### 25. August.

On Wednesday <note>original: "Mercurij die", literally "the day of Mercury," the standard Latin term for Wednesday.</note>, the Lord Doctor BESOLD, considering an excursion for the sake of his spirit—by which he might refresh the fatigue of a mind oppressed by constant studies and forestall an encroaching infirmity of health—chose the city of Eichstätt <note>original: "Aichstadianam vrbem". Eichstätt was an important cultural and religious center in Bavaria.</note> for this leisure. It was a destination well-suited both for its convenient proximity and for its many churches, which were appropriate for his devotion. He prepared for the journey there. At the start of dinner, he was in high spirits, but the meal's conclusion brought him a sadder end; for, seized by a sudden chill, he hastened to bed and yielded to the beginnings of the disease. The causes were clear: trusting too much in his natural strength, he had contracted a stomach ailment from cheaper food and a more lax diet; however, at the beginning, these things did not hinder his vigorous nature.

### 26. August.

At daybreak <note>original: "Renafcente Aurorâ", literally "with Dawn being reborn."</note>, he began the journey along with his daughter and his wife (who, having traveled as far as Pappenheim, had taken her dinner at the home of the preacher). He was accompanied by us for the sake of honor and our promised duty. He spent his time there more cheerfully, refreshing himself greatly with spiritual matters, especially by viewing the <term>relics</term><note>original: "Lipsanis". This refers to the physical remains of saints or holy objects, which Besold, a recent convert to Catholicism, would have found spiritually significant.</note> of the Saints, and vis-

<meta>catchword: These</meta>

...to be seen and venerated, which the Reverend Father Albert Curtius, of the Society of Jesus, showed him here and there.

->27. August<-

The following day, he toured the sacred buildings with remarkable devotion, and having been refreshed by the Heavenly Bread <note>original: "Cœleſti pane", a common reference to receiving the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> among the Reverend Capuchin Fathers, he held nothing more important than—disregarding his own well-being—committing himself once again to the business of others, which he had barely let out of his hands. Thus, he could not be persuaded by any pleas (not even those of the Illustrious Bishop, who had kindly sent a carriage to invite him) to indulge his old age by seeking a longer break from his studies and relaxing slightly the intensity of his continuous labor. 

He gave as the reason for his haste the need to send legal advice <note>original: "Consilium", referring to formal legal counsel, as Besold was a renowned jurist.</note> to someone as quickly as possible. Thus, to a man equal to the greatest affairs of state, even the personal matters of individuals were close to his heart and concern. He therefore returned home. Immediately upon arrival, he took to his bed, seized by a slight fever <note>original: "febriculâ"</note>, which was followed by a heavy catarrh <note>original: "Catarrhus craſſior", a term used in the 17th century to describe an inflammation of the mucus membranes, often involving a buildup of phlegm.</note>. Nevertheless, he was not so immediately deprived of his strength that he did not occasionally tire of the bed and sit at our table, or walk about his room. But the minor illness grew stronger over time, and finally it degenerated into a loosening of the bowels <note>original: "ſolutionem alui", likely referring to dysentery or severe diarrhea.</note> and a lethal loathing <note>original: "lethale faſtidium"</note> of the stomach.

But the Mother of Mercy preferred to repay the affection of her son—for this venerable old man had recently declared himself such using a solemn formula in a large gathering of young men—with a better gift than he had asked for. She chose to grant him the salvation of his soul, by which he might travel to see her in heaven, and to wash away any remaining stains of sin by means of this relatively brief illness.

Meanwhile, the fame of his name—which had already spread throughout all Europe and through the courts of all the Great—stirred a longing for him in every person. He had been summoned many times before this to the service of our most invincible Emperor <note>Likely referring to the Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II or III.</note>, and he was called once again now. At the same time, he was also sought after as a political counselor for Innsbruck <note>original: "Oenipontum", the Latin name for Innsbruck, the capital of Tyrol.</note>. Indeed, Italy too longed to be brightened by the rays of his presence; it seemed to her that she would be blessed again, as if by a second Cato <note>Referring to Cato the Elder or Cato the Younger, Roman statesmen who were symbols of integrity, wisdom, and traditional virtue.</note>.

The Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope, at this time Urban VIII.</note>, having offered him the primary professorship at Bologna <note>original: "Bononiensium". Bologna was home to one of the most prestigious law faculties in Europe.</note> with a very large salary, sent him at the same time a bull <note>An official papal document or decree.</note> marked with his own signature. By this document, if he were unable to undertake the journey to Bologna, the Pope granted him the administration of the provostship of Stuttgart <note>original: "Stutgardianæ". A provostship was a lucrative and high-ranking ecclesiastical administrative position.</note>, which was quite wealthy.

Moved with very little joy by such news, he showed that he was now hoping for greater and heavenly things. He was doubtless suspecting the approach of death, not indeed out of fear (which does not affect a wise man), but in the hope of an end to his miseries. Now despising all earthly things, he sought medicine from the heavenly apothecary <note>original: "cœlesti pharmacopœo"; a metaphor for God or Christ as the ultimate healer of the soul.</note>.

...called to the son, he said the case was hopeless, and that no means of recovery remained. Who could express the grief this response caused everyone? Yet, surely, if we listen to Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Roman Stoic philosopher. His works were frequently quoted by 17th-century scholars like Besold.</note>, he says: "We must hold our friends as if we were about to lose them, and lose them as if we still held them" <note>original: "Oportet, vt Amicos habeamus tanquam amissuri; amittamus, tanquam habeamus."</note>.

### September 12th.

On Sunday, the requested doctor arrived. He kept our minds in a state of distressing doubt with his vague and ambiguous <note>original: "amphibologicis", meaning double-worded or open to multiple interpretations.</note> answers about the patient’s health. He explicitly offered no hope, yet he wished to keep fear at bay even more. Nevertheless, he revealed to the **Reverend Father Bisselius** <note>Johann Bisselius (1601–1682), a Jesuit scholar and poet who recorded Besold's conversion and final days.</note>, who was visiting the sick man frequently, that **Doctor Hoefer**'s <note>Wolfgang Hoefer (1614–1681), a prominent court physician.</note> hopeless opinion was based on significant evidence. 

After administering the medicines that the desperate situation required, the doctor did not fail in his duties; he worked tirelessly for the health of such a great man—a man whom the Fates would only take from this world amidst universal sorrow. Therefore, he urgently pressed that the patient should fortify himself with the **Holy Communion** <term>Synaxis: A Greek term (σύναξις) meaning "assembly," used here in a liturgical sense to refer to the reception of the Eucharist as part of the last rites.</term>. He arranged for the **Fathers of the Society** <note>The Jesuits, or the Society of Jesus, who were attending to Besold's spiritual needs following his conversion to Catholicism.</note> to advise the patient of this, so that he himself would not have to be the one to deliver the "death sentence" to the sick man by his own word. He feared being as unwelcome to everyone with such an omen as men usually are when bringing bad...

the intermediaries are just as serious as the authors themselves. They all agreed, and the *most distinguished Besold* himself summoned *Reverend Father Georgius Liprandus of the Society of Jesus* <note>Georg Liprandt (1591–1648), a Jesuit theologian and professor at the University of Ingolstadt.</note>, a Professor of Theology, to whom he was accustomed to confess. He voluntarily purified his conscience with Catholic piety and diligence, professing that he would die not only with a calm mind, but even a joyful one, provided that his little daughter (whom he had obtained from **GOD** through a miracle) were placed in safety and in the free practice of the Roman religion.

->*September 13th.*<-

In the evening around six o'clock, the *Most Venerable Sacrament* <term>The Eucharist: In the Catholic tradition of the time, the "Viaticum" or final communion was brought to the dying in a formal procession.</term> was brought in with a crowded procession. In the presence of the *Magnificent Rector*, the *Barons*, as well as the *Professors and many students*, he received it with great devotion. When the sacred rites were completed, having summoned the *Professors* to his bed, he gave clear signs of joy by word of mouth that he had been led to the knowledge and embrace of the true faith by divine goodness. To all the *Academic Fathers* <note>Refers to the senior faculty and governing body of the university.</note>, he commended his daughter to be educated in a Catholic and pious manner, and his wife to be converted to the orthodox faith. With a deep groan, he exclaimed that it would be a source of the greatest [grief...] <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "dolo-" suggests the Latin "dolori," meaning pain or grief.</note>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Christopher Besold’s final hours in September 1638. [...great] grief in his final struggle <term>agone: refers to the 'death agony' or the final spiritual and physical struggle before passing</term>; unless he were first certain that this would happen, expressing it in these formal words:

> <note>original German: "wann ich disen Trost nit gewiß haben kan/ würdt ich wol mit grossem Schmertzen scheiden."</note> "If I cannot have this comfort for certain, I will surely depart with great pain."

Therefore, he begged his wife and daughter to promise him this as his final request <term>ultimā petitionem: a dying wish or formal deathbed plea</term>. Both obeyed his words, and his wife openly declared that just as she had always been obedient to her lord husband, she would not refuse his request in this matter either, but wished to fulfill her husband's last will <term>voluntatem: a person's final intent or testament</term> to the best of her ability—provided that she were prepared with sufficient instruction <term>instructione: specifically, religious instruction or catechism in the Catholic faith</term> for a matter of such great importance. 

The minds of those standing by were remarkably moved by this sad conversation; tears were even wrung from many great men. Soon, the mourning of the women broke out into disordered wailing—for how could such grief be absent during the tearing apart of such close intimacy? The silence that had been maintained to hear the sum of his speech dissolved into various lamentations; the whole house echoed with sorrowful voices. 

But who would not grieve for one whose life is in danger, who by his virtues and learning has long ago earned immortality? One of whom it is permitted to say that he was a miracle to his contemporaries and an example to posterity, and with whom a great Treasury of Learning <term>eruditionis Thesaurus: a common metaphor for a polymath or a scholar whose mind contains a 'treasury' of knowledge</term> would perish without an heir! But the excessive noise of the mourners was restrained...

### September 14th

As this day dawned, even a small glimmer of hope for his recovery seemed to shine forth. Prayers and sacrifices <note>referring to the Mass</note> were offered by religious families <note>religious orders or communities</note> for the sick man, for whose improved health everyone’s vows burned with fervor. Doctor Ernest <note>likely a local physician</note>, unswayed by any prayers or promises, departed for home after assigning the necessary medicines to the patient; he judged, naturally, that it was in vain to strive against fate. This was especially so since old age is an incurable disease—though Lord Besold had maintained a vigorous life until his 61st year, subject to no ailments except for gout <term>podagra: a painful form of arthritis, historically known as the "disease of kings" and associated with aging</term>. Doctor Hoofer also, a man most excellent in medical theory, repeated his prognosis of the funeral that was soon to follow, unless heavenly causes should intervene. 

But alas! How fate plays with men, even at the cost of life, and eludes their hopes! The patient, who had eaten nothing for four days and was refreshed only by sleep and drink—which was the very peak of the disease—once he had tasted a small morsel...

And now he began to desire more familiar conversation. But indeed, he was about to bid his final farewell to the world and its inhabitants. For from that time on, he considered nothing of the sort; nor did he wish to take any further medicines or restoratives <term>confortativa: strengthening tonics or cordials meant to revive the spirits and physical strength</term>. Without a doubt, he had shaken off the desire for life—which, according to the philosopher Seneca, is a shameful thing in an old man <note>original: "Turpis... seni est." Besold, a scholar, here aligns his death with Stoic and Christian ideals</note>—and looking toward death, he resigned himself entirely to the Divine will.

Throughout the entire time he was bedridden, he displayed great examples of virtue. With these, he overcame the bitter envy of the heretics <note>the Protestant critics who had attacked Besold after his conversion to Catholicism in 1635</note>, and through his pious patience, he frustrated their long-circulated slanders—which had even spread to foreign shores—aimed at attacking his spotless reputation and the purity of his life.

He showed an absolute, extreme obedience toward his Spiritual Father <note>his confessor or spiritual advisor</note>, never resisting by so much as a gesture anything the Father had advised. His devotion was truly Catholic and religious. His patience was of a rare kind, and his resolve could be imitated by few. His constancy was beyond what is human: he was not moved by the pains of his illness, nor by the tidings of death, nor even by the unrestrained wailing of his wife and daughter as they threw themselves across his bed. He remained unbroken in spirit, his expression entirely unchanged, and...

### September 15th.

After the middle of the night, around two in the morning, he seemed to be struggling for his final breath; therefore, Father Bisselius <note>Johannes Bisselius (1601–1682), a Jesuit scholar and poet who was a close friend of Besold</note>, who was usually assisting him, was summoned immediately by my superior, Master Johann Sebastian Küchler. Meanwhile, Master Georg Ludwig Lindenspür tended to the readiness of his soul with comforts, and, stirring him to persevere in the devotion he had begun, piously exhorted him to perform those acts worthy of a dying man; but the sick man was able to ask whether that time was already at hand (uttering the formal words: *Is it then time?* <note>original: "ist es dann an dem?" Besold slips into his native German here</note>), as if he knew that this final limit had not yet been set for him. 

We all crowded around the bed, hardly present to ourselves because of our grief, about to witness the sad scene of human life; soon the aforementioned Father also arrived; and by all pious means—through exhortations, prayers, and consolations—he raised the sick man’s spirits toward the hope of the heavenly homeland. # September 17th.

The **burial** <term>depositio: Literally a "laying down," specifically the rite of entombing a body</term> having been appointed for **Friday** <note>original Latin: "diem Veneris"; the day of Venus</note>: after the ceremony was prepared with solemn order and procession, around eight o'clock the funeral was led to the **Parish Church of the Blessed Virgin** <note>This likely refers to the Frauenkirche in Ingolstadt, where Besold was a professor</note>. There, he was buried in the heart of the choir, so that she whom he had served as a devotee while living might receive him into her bosom now that he was dead. Thus those lips and that tongue, celebrated throughout the whole world, have yielded as food for worms. Thus the head honored by **Princes** was given over to decay. A sad spectacle! What sensible person, even slightly moved by public calamities, would not grieve? For whom even the inanimate things of the Universe mourn? The very sky, composed for mourning, **wept** for the funeral, gloomy with rains during the leading of the procession. The sun itself mourned this **sun of the learned** (whose rays even now illuminate countless volumes), veiled behind a sadder cloud; whereas the days before and after, dissolved and open in cheerfulness, had smiled with clear air. Therefore, all the **Sacrifices** <note>original Latin: "Sacrificia"; in this Catholic context, referring to the Sacrifice of the Mass offered for the deceased</note> were devoted to his eternal rest, and honor was paid to his **departed spirit** <term>Manibus: The "Manes" or ancestral spirits of the dead in Roman tradition, here used classically to refer to the soul of the deceased</term> by the prayers of all. The tomb was watered with abundant torrents of **tears**. The greatest part of this sorrow was ours, nor [was] anyone to us...

Because of his reputation for wisdom, Numa Pompilius was called to the throne from Cures, a town of the Sabines; he was all the more remarkable as a King because he refused the kingdom for a long time. He tamed Rome—a city then fierce with arms—through religion, or rather, through superstition. He did this by establishing sacred rites and priesthoods, while pretending to have nightly meetings with the Goddess Egeria. He claimed that he established these sacred and other institutions under her instruction. <note>Numa Pompilius was the legendary second king of Rome, credited with moving the city's focus from warfare to religious law.</note> *Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book 2; Livy, Book 1.* Regarding the Roman Kings, see *Florus*, as well as *Puteanus*; and on the books of Numa, see *Guylandinus in his work On Papyrus, pages 370 and 373, etc.*

His successor, Ancus Marcius, studiously maintaining the institutions of his grandfather Numa, cultivated both religion and peace.

### CHAPTER VIII.

# CONCERNING THE THIRD MONARCHY,

### *namely that of the Greeks.*

> Through these great victories, Alexander brought under his rule almost all the lands extending toward the rising sun. <note>A poetic reference to the East; Alexander's empire reached as far as the Punjab region of modern-day India.</note> And thus he transferred the supreme authority of the Empire from Asia to Europe; *and established the Third Monarchy in the Year of the World 3724.* <note>The "Year of the World" (Anno Mundi) 3724 in this chronological system corresponds to roughly 330 BCE.</note>

It was called the Kingdom of the Greeks, however, not because the head of the Kingdom was always located in Greece, or remained under a single King, or had its seat in only one city—as was the case with the Kingdom of the Assyrians, the Chaldeans, and the Persians—but because it had its beginning and was birthed by Alexander, who was Greek by nation; and after his death, it was divided among his friends, <note>The "friends" or *Diadochi* (Successors) were Alexander's generals, such as Ptolemy, Seleucus, and Antigonus, who carved the empire into several Hellenistic kingdoms.</note> who were likewise Greeks. *Tornielli, <note>Agostino Tornielli (1543–1622) was an Italian priest and scholar known for his works on biblical chronology.</note> Year of the World 3724.*

And in the end, he struck the ram itself and broke its two horns—the Medes and the Persians—casting him under his feet and subjugating both 'horns' to his own Empire."

### CHAPTER IX.

## ON THE DIVISION OF THE THIRD MONAR-
### *chy.*

The appearance of the **Third Monarchy** <note>In the "Four Monarchies" theory of history common in this era, the Third Monarchy refers to the Grecian/Macedonian Empire established by Alexander.</note> is recognized as being different from the previous two. For although it took its beginning from a single head, once that head was torn away, it shattered into diverse members, clearly separated from each other and nearly equal in power.

### CHAPTER X.
## CONCERNING THE KINGS OF SYRIA.

**Seleucus**, the first of this name, who is also called **Nicanor** <note>original: "Nicanor," meaning "the Victorious" in Greek.</note>; obtained the Kingdom of **Syria**, and afterward also of **Asia**. For having obtained the command of the **Elephants** from **Alexander**; after his death, he was first appointed by **Perdiccas** to lead the wing of the King's household cavalry; then by **Antipater** as governor of the **Babylonian satrapy**.

While he <note>Referring to the rival general Antigonus Monophthalmus, who is implied by the historical context.</note> insolently demanded the accounts of this province, **Seleucus**, fearing a greater danger, fled to **Ptolemy** in **Egypt**. There, having been received with the greatest kindness and supplied with troops, he not only recovered **Babylon**, but, having subdued the **Bactrians** <note>People of a region in Central Asia, modern-day Afghanistan and Uzbekistan.</note>, he extended the borders of his Empire as far as **India** in a most successful course of victories.

Once this was discovered by the physician **Erasistratus** <note>A famous ancient Greek anatomist and royal physician who realized the prince's "illness" was actually lovesickness by observing his pulse when Stratonice entered the room.</note>, although his father willingly surrendered her to him, Antiochus was nevertheless overcome by shame and modesty and did not accept her; it was only after his father's death, which soon followed, that he first came into her embrace.

<margin>„</margin>**Antiochus**, surnamed **Theos** <note>original: "Theos," meaning "the God," a title granted to him by the citizens of Miletus for delivering them from a tyrant.</note>, succeeded him. He fought in a long and difficult war with **Ptolemy Philadelphus** <note>Ptolemy II, the ruler of Egypt and patron of the Library of Alexandria.</note>. After being reconciled to him through a marriage with **Berenice** <note>Ptolemy's daughter; this marriage was intended to seal a peace treaty between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic empires.</note>, he stirred up a new and domestic hatred in **Laodice**, his first wife. Although she had been neglected for some time and held in the position of a concubine, once he finally received her back into the Palace, he was killed by her with poison.

This man was the first and only one of the **Seleucids** <note>The Greek-Macedonian dynasty that ruled much of the Near East after the death of Alexander the Great.</note> to have two wives at the same time. From these, **Laodice** gave birth to **Seleucus Callinicus** and **Antiochus**, who was given the surname **Hierax** <note>original: "Hierax," meaning "the Hawk," a name given to him because of his predatory and ambitious nature.</note> on account of his greed. See **Vossius** <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a prominent Dutch scholar and historian.</note>, page 71, on the Greek historians; and also see there concerning **Annius** <note>Likely referring to Annius of Viterbo, a scholar known for historical commentaries, though often associated with forgeries.</note>.

<margin>„</margin>**Seleucus Callinicus** <note>meaning "the Beautiful Victor."</note> began his reign under the omens of parricide <note>Here used in the broader sense of the murder of close relatives.</note>. For having obtained the Kingdom through the cunning of his mother, he permitted her to kill his stepmother **Berenice** along with her son. But he, together with all his descendants, paid the heaviest penalties for this crime. For besides the fact that he waged war amidst constant dangers, the **Parthians** and **Bactrians** first revolted then, and soon even the **Armenians** followed, establishing independent kingdoms. Likewise, the family of **Phileterus** <note>The founder of the Attalid dynasty of Pergamum.</note>, which had been suppressed before, grew by gradually seizing the borders of the **Syrian Kingdom**; it grew to such an extent that, through the **Romans**, once the **Seleucids** had been ejected from Nearer Asia, that family claimed the occupied land for themselves.

## Of Egypt.

The Kings of Egypt, starting from Ptolemy, the first founder of the family, all called themselves "Ptolemies." Under this king lived Demetrius Phalereus <note>An Athenian statesman and philosopher who was instrumental in the founding of the Library of Alexandria.</note>, *see Vossius, On the Greek Historians, folio 57.*

## ON THE KINGS
### of Egypt.

The Kings of Egypt, starting from Ptolemy, the first founder of the family, all called themselves "Ptolemies." During his reign lived Demetrius Phalereus <note>A statesman and scholar from Athens who was instrumental in the creation of the Library of Alexandria.</note>; see Vossius <note>Gerhard Johann Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar and humanist.</note> on the Greek Historians, page 57.

This Ptolemy, who was later honored with the surname "the Great," was commonly said to be the son of Lagus. However, Lagus had received Arsinoë as a wife from Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon.</note>, the father of Alexander; she was already pregnant by the King, and from this union, as Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century CE Greek traveler and geographer.</note> records, Ptolemy was born.

Because of the loyalty he had shown under the father Philip, he was accepted by Alexander among his bodyguards; he followed Alexander into Asia, and brought the murderer Bessus <note>A Persian satrap who killed Darius III and was eventually captured and executed by Alexander's forces.</note> into [his] power...

# SYNOPSIS

The Senate, having been persuaded by Gnaeus Pompey <note>Pompey the Great, a leading Roman general and statesman</note>, ensured that he [Ptolemy Auletes] was restored to his throne through Aulus Gabinius. Cicero writes extensively on this matter in *Book 1 of his Letters to Friends to Lentulus* <note>original: "libr. 1. famil. Epist. ad Lentulum"</note> and in his *Oration for Rabirius* <note>original: "orat. pro Rabir." referring to the trial of Rabirius Postumus, who was involved in the Egyptian finances</note>. Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note> also noted that, during this King’s reign, the annual revenues of the Egyptian Kingdom were 12,500 talents. When calculated into our modern currency, this amounts to 7,500,000 crowns. *But one should consult the commentary there; see Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon, a renowned Renaissance scholar who wrote famous commentaries on Strabo</note>.*

Ptolemy Dionysius <note>Ptolemy XIII, the son of Auletes</note>, honored by his father’s will with the Kingdom and a marriage to his sister Cleopatra <note>The famous Cleopatra VII</note>, received Pompey as a guardian appointed by the Roman Senate. However, after the Battle of Pharsalia <note>The decisive battle in 48 BC where Julius Caesar defeated Pompey</note>, when Pompey fled to him for refuge, Ptolemy had him murdered by Achillas. This was done at the instigation of his tutor Theodotus and the eunuch Pothinus. He then sent Pompey’s head, along with his signet ring, to the victorious Caesar as a pledge of friendship.

Finally, he [Ptolemy XIII] waged war against his sister Cleopatra. Although Caesar wished to settle the dispute peacefully, the King attempted to defend himself with arms. Having been defeated by Caesar in battle, he perished in the Nile; his ship was weighed down and sunk by the great number of people attempting to flee.

Caesar, however, did not reduce Egypt to the status of a Roman province at that time, but instead granted the Kingdom to Cleopatra and her younger brother <note>Ptolemy XIV</note>.

Cleopatra indeed, the last Queen of Egypt, disdaining the youth of her brother <note>Ptolemy XIII, who was her co-ruler and brother-husband</note> and burning entirely with love for Caesar; after Scipio <note>Metellus Scipio, a supporter of Pompey who led the resistance against Caesar in Africa</note> had been defeated in Africa, she visited him in Rome and, a son having been born to her, she gave him a name from him <note>Cleopatra named her son Caesarion, meaning "Little Caesar," claiming him to be the son of Julius Caesar</note>.

After Caesar was assassinated, when she was called into suspicion by Antony <note>Mark Antony, the Roman general and member of the Triumvirate</note> on the grounds that she had aided Cassius <note>Gaius Cassius Longinus, one of the lead conspirators in Caesar's assassination</note> with money, she not only appeased him but also completely drove him mad with her lustful submission and flatteries. Indeed, she so overflowed with luxury that she surpassed Antony in the splendor of a banquet—specifically by means of a pearl, the value of which was reckoned at ten million sesterces <note>An enormous sum in Roman currency; the "pearl story" is a famous legend of Cleopatra's extravagance</note>, which she dissolved in vinegar and swallowed in a single draught. *Macrobius, Saturnalia, Book 3, Chapter 17.*

And now claiming everything for herself, she proceeded not only with other crimes but also arranged, through Antony, for the murder of her brother-husband <note>Ptolemy XIV</note> and her sister Arsinoë. Then, having been hailed as "Queen of Kings," she finally drove Antony himself to divorce Octavia <note>Octavia the Younger, the sister of Octavian (Augustus) and Antony’s legal wife</note> and to receive her into his marriage bed. Taking this very poorly, Augustus Caesar <note>Octavian, later the first Roman Emperor</note>, the brother of Octavia, forced Cleopatra and Antony to bring death upon themselves. *Plutarch, Life of Antony; Dio Cassius, Book 50 and following.* He then made Egypt (which at that time was all that remained of the Greek Monarchy <note>Referring to the Hellenistic kingdoms established by the successors of Alexander the Great</note>) a province of the Roman People.

Alexander <note>Alexander V of Macedon</note>, in order to avenge the murder of his mother <note>Thessalonice, who had been killed by her other son, Antipater II</note>, called upon Pyrrhus, the King of the Epirotes <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus, a famous general and cousin of Alexander the Great</note>, to enter Greece. Pyrrhus, as payment for the aid he brought, occupied a large portion of Macedonia; consequently, he soon appeared as someone to be feared by Alexander. Therefore, to cast Pyrrhus out of Macedonia again, Alexander implored the aid of **Demetrius Polyorcetes** <note>Demetrius I of Macedon, known as "Polyorcetes" or "the Besieger" for his military tactics</note>. Demetrius soon set to work to eject both Antipater and Pyrrhus from Macedonia. Therefore Lysimachus <note>One of Alexander the Great's former generals and the King of Thrace</note>, who was the father-in-law of Antipater, fearing the power of Demetrius, persuaded his son-in-law to return to favor with his brother Alexander.

Demetrius, however, perceived this plan, and since Alexander was also making his own plots to ensnare Demetrius, he decided to strike first to prevent the danger looming over him. He killed Alexander through an ambush. He then excused the murder to the Macedonians and spoke at length about the tyranny of Cassander and his sons; by this means, he brought it about that he was named King of Macedonia. Lysimachus also, while he was hard-pressed by war with the Thracians, killed his own son-in-law Antipater, so that he would not be forced to fight Demetrius on his behalf.

<margin>,, ,, ,,</margin> But Pyrrhus, the King of Epirus, having corrupted the army of Demetrius, drove him into flight and took possession of the Kingdom of Macedonia.

<header>SUMMARY</header>

It is found recorded of **Marcus Atilius Regulus** <note>A Roman general and consul (died c. 250 BCE) who became a legendary symbol of Roman honor and sacrifice.</note> that, after capturing Tunis and other Punic <note>The Romans used the term "Punic" (from the Latin *Poeni*) to refer to the Carthaginians, due to their Phoenician ancestry.</note> towns by force, he laid siege to Carthage. However, he was defeated by **Xanthippus the Spartan**, a general who had come to the aid of the Carthaginians, and fell into the power of the enemy. Yet his noble character shone more brightly in disaster than it had in victory. For when he was sent to Rome to negotiate an exchange of prisoners, he argued against a proposal that would have been beneficial for himself and his family, but useless for his Fatherland. Then, lest he should break the oath of faith given to the enemy, he returned to Carthage, where he was put to death with every kind of torture—earning no less praise for his courage than for his loyalty. *See Heinrich Meibom, in his notes on Sleidanus’s* On the Four Monarchies, *Book 1, page 80; and Joachim Camerarius,* Spare Hours, *century 2, chapter 58.*

While that war continued, the Romans fought successfully at sea for the very first time under the Consul **Gaius Duilius** in Sicily. <note>original: *C. Duilio Conſule*. Duilius won Rome's first major naval victory at the Battle of Mylae in 260 BCE by using the "corvus," a boarding bridge that allowed Roman soldiers to fight as if on land.</note> *Livy, Book 17.*

At length, that war was settled after it had lasted twenty-three years, *Orosius, Book 4, chapter 11,* under these conditions: that the Carthaginians should withdraw from Sicily, Sardinia, and the other islands, and should pay a fixed tribute to the Roman People for twenty years.

**Portius Cato**: <note>Marcus Porcius Cato, known as Cato the Elder (234–149 BCE), a Roman statesman and the first to write history in Latin.</note> *Cicero in his Brutus*, <note>original: *in Bruto*. The Romans were then entangled in new wars against the Falisci, the Ligurians, the Illyrians, and the Insubrian and Boian Gauls. <note>These conflicts occurred between 241 and 218 BCE as Rome expanded its control over the Italian peninsula and the Adriatic coast.</note> *See Livy, Book 20; Florus, Book 2, chapter 3, etc.; Polybius, Book 2.*

When these were finally conquered, the **Second Punic War** broke out, twenty-four years after peace had been established. Its leader was **Hannibal**, who captured Saguntum and, moving through the Spanish territories into Gaul and from there into Italy, overcame the Roman people in three battles: at the Ticinus, at the river Trebia, and at Lake Trasimene. <note>These three victories in 218–217 BCE allowed Hannibal to threaten the heart of Roman power.</note> *Livy, Book 10 <note>The author likely refers to the lost summaries or a specific edition, as the Second Punic War begins in Livy's Book 21.</note>, etc.; Appian, On the Affairs of Hannibal; Silius Italicus, Book 4 and following.*

**Quintus Fabius Maximus** was then appointed Dictator, and having set out against the enemy, he broke Hannibal’s strength by means of delay. <note>Fabius earned the nickname "Cunctator" (The Delayer) for his strategy of avoiding pitched battles and wearing down Hannibal’s supplies through a war of attrition.</note> *Plutarch, in his Life of Fabius Maximus; Silius Italicus, Books 6 and 7.*

Afterward, the Roman people suffered a massive slaughter at **Cannae**, <note>Fought in 216 BCE, this remains one of the most famous tactical masterpieces in military history and Rome's most devastating defeat.</note> which indeed stirred up such great panic in the city that many of the more powerful citizens considered flight and the abandonment of Italy. *Livy, Book 22; Polybius, Book 5; Silius Italicus, Book 9.*

But at Capua, Hannibal found his own Cannae; <note>original: *Sed Annibal Capuæ, Cannas inuenit*. This historical proverb suggests that the luxuries and comforts Hannibal's army enjoyed while wintering in the city of Capua ruined their discipline and military edge, ultimately leading to their downfall just as Cannae had nearly ruined Rome.</note>

For his strength <note>Referring to Hannibal’s army.</note> was softened by the delights of Campania, <note>original: *Campanis delitijs*. This refers to the "luxuries of Capua," a famous historical trope suggesting that the comforts of the city of Capua made Hannibal's soldiers soft and undisciplined.</note> *Florus, Book 2, chapter 5.* Marcus Claudius Marcellus, in a second battle fought at Nola, showed that Hannibal could be defeated. From that point, a new war arose out of the war. After the death of Hiero, King of Syracuse, Hieronymus—the heir to the kingdom but not to his father's loyalty—had defected to Hannibal. Therefore, the <term>Consul<note>One of the two highest-ranking elected political and military leaders in the Roman Republic.</note></term> Marcellus brought war against the Syracusans. 

The city of Syracuse was defended no less by the genius of **Archimedes** than by the weapons of its citizens. After Marcellus had unsuccessfully besieged it for a long time, the city was finally overcome by its own negligence and luxury; he captured it unexpectedly by night. The victor’s moderation increased the glory of his victory, for he spared both the city and its people. As for **Archimedes**, who had fallen during the initial incursion of the soldiers, Marcellus paid honor to him in death since he could not do so while he was alive. <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) was a Greek mathematician and inventor whose war machines held the Romans at bay. Legend says he was killed by a soldier while focused on a mathematical diagram, much to Marcellus's regret.</note> 

Following this, Laevinus pacified the Sicilians and made Sicily the first <term>Province<note>original: *prouinciam*. A territory outside Italy under the direct administration of a Roman governor.</note></term> of the Roman People. *Livy, Book 25; Silius Italicus, Book 14; Plutarch, Life of Marcellus; Cicero, Against Verres, 4.*

But Roman affairs were not successful everywhere at that time. In Spain, the two Scipios, <note>Publius and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio, the father and uncle of the future Scipio Africanus.</note> despite often managing matters well, were finally slain by **Hasdrubal**, the brother of Hannibal. *Livy, Book 26 and following.*

[The Roman spirit] was stronger and even more high-minded. Hannibal was nearly at the gates of the city; and yet Publius Cornelius Scipio—still a young man and acting as the avenger of his father and uncle <note>Scipio’s father, Publius, and uncle, Gnaeus, had both been killed in battle against the Carthaginians in Spain in 211 BCE.</note>—was sent into Spain. Yet he gained more through his self-restraint than through his victory; for when a noble girl of extraordinary beauty was brought to him, he returned her untouched to her betrothed. <note>This famous episode is known as the "Continence of Scipio." By returning the captive princess to her fiancé, Scipio won the loyalty of many local Spanish tribes.</note> The reputation of such virtue and integrity won over the Spaniards to him in a wonderful way. Consequently, he put Hasdrubal <note>original: *Afdrubalem*. Hasdrubal Barca was Hannibal's brother.</note> to flight from Spain and made it the first province on the continent.

Nor were matters less successful in Italy. Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, the <term>Proconsul<note>A former consul whose military command was extended to act as a governor or general in a specific territory.</note></term>, after Hannibal had meanwhile been driven back from the city, received the surrender of Capua. Punishment was exacted from their Senate; nevertheless, so that Capua might never be able to stage a rebellion again, their land was confiscated. Every magistrate, their Senate, and their public council were abolished, leaving behind no image of a <term>Republic<note>original: *Reipublicæ*. Referring here to the city’s independent political structure or "commonwealth."</note></term>. Instead, it was determined that the city should merely be a place for gathering and storing crops—a shelter for speakers, a marketplace for peasants, and a cellar and granary for the Campanian territory. *Cicero, Against Rullus; Velleius Paterculus, Book 2.*

He, therefore, finally set out from Sicily into Africa, and he proved by the deed itself what he had predicted to the Senate; for the Carthaginians, defeated by him in several battles and afflicted by very many losses, recalled Hannibal. After peace was made with the Carthaginians, the Romans were occupied with wars throughout Italy, Istria, and Lusitania <note>A region in the western Iberian Peninsula, primarily modern-day Portugal.</note>, which Orosius briefly touches upon in *Book 4, Chapter 10*. Once Greece was pacified, Antiochus—nicknamed "the Great"—the King of Asia and Syria, brought war against the Romans at the urging of Hannibal. Antiochus was defeated on land and sea through the strategy and courage of the general Lucius Scipio (the full brother of Africanus) and the advice of Africanus himself, who served as his <term>Legate<note>A high-ranking military officer or deputy who served directly under a commander or the Senate.</note></term>. Consequently, Antiochus was forced to seek peace.

The Third Punic War also arose—concerning which Appian writes in his *Libyan Wars*, Eutropius in *Book 4*, Florus in *Book 2, Chapter 15*, and Orosius in *Book 4, Chapter 22*. ### OF UNIVERSAL HISTORY.

After Julius Caesar was killed, a Triumvirate <term>Triumvirate: A political alliance of three men; specifically the Second Triumvirate (43–33 BCE) formed to "restore" the Roman state.</term> for organizing the Republic was established; and the supreme power passed to Mark Antony, Caius Octavius, and Marcus Lepidus. They wore each other out with mutual wars, until finally Lepidus was removed from the triumvirate and exiled, and Antony was also defeated.

II. Octavius, therefore—the grandson of Julius Caesar's sister <note>Octavius (later Augustus) was the great-nephew and posthumously adopted son of Julius Caesar. The author refers to his lineage through Caesar's sister, Julia.</note>—once Antony was removed, held the Empire alone. Thus, he is counted as the second Roman Emperor. Regarding him, one must understand that most famous "Royal Law" <term>Royal Law: Known in Latin as the *Lex Regia*, this was the legal fiction that the Roman people had transferred all their sovereign power and authority to the Emperor.</term>, which is mentioned in *the first law of the Digest regarding the Constitution of Princes [l. 1. ff. de Constit. princ.], as I reported in my short book on the Monarchy, chapter 4, number 5.*

The reason why the Roman people so easily accepted this remarkable change is explained by Cornelius Tacitus, briefly and sharply as is his way, when in *Book 1 of his Annals, he says:* "Once he had seduced the soldiers with gifts, the People with food supplies, and everyone with the sweetness of peace, he began to rise up gradually and draw into himself the duties of the Senate, the magistrates, and the laws, with no one opposing him. Since the most defiant had fallen in battle or by proscription <note>Proscription: The state-sanctioned murder or banishment of political enemies whose property was then confiscated.</note>, the rest of the nobles were elevated with wealth and honors in proportion to how ready they were for servitude; and having prospered from the new state of affairs, they [preferred] safe and..."

Two years later, he <note>Referring to Julius Caesar.</note> again crossed the Rhine by bridge, a little above the place where he had previously led his army across. ### III. Claudius Tiberius Nero

...covered with [wild beast] skins, they died by the tearing of dogs, or were fixed to crosses, or destined for the flames: so that when the day came to an end, they were burned to provide light during the night.

This burning, moreover, was carried out in this manner: Those wretched people were dressed in garments of pitch-wood, papyrus, and wax; then, as they stood at the stake, a hook was fixed through their throats so that they could not move their heads to spill the pitch or avoid the fire. ## XVIII. Commodus Antoninus

**Commodus Antoninus**, the son of Marcus, began his reign in the **Year of Christ 182**, though he was not yet of a mature age for the Empire. Consequently, he was corrupted by sycophants <note>The Latin *assentatoribus* refers to "yes-men" or flatterers who encourage a ruler's worst instincts.</note>, and he came to resemble Domitian far more than his own father. He spent his life in the most disgraceful manner, indulging in every kind of depravity and cruelty.
<note>original: "Lamprid." referring to Aelius Lampridius, one of the credited authors of the *Augustan History*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note>

Yet, despite being such a man, he never attempted anything against the Christians. From this, it clearly appears that such a monster was sent by an angry God as a form of vengeance for Christian blood. He vented his savage cruelty so immensely upon the Senators, Magistrates, and the People—who had treated the Christians so poorly—as if to punish them.
<note>original: "Baron. Anno Christi 182. n. 3." referring to the *Ecclesiastical Annals* by Cardinal Cesare Baronio (1538–1607).</note>
Consequently, during this time, the affairs of the Christians and the profession of the faith increased daily. Especially in the greatest cities, entire multitudes and whole households came to the faith.
<note>original: "Niceph. lib 5. cap. 26." referring to the *Ecclesiastical History* of Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine historian.</note>

Under his reign, **Saint Irenaeus** flourished as the Bishop of Lyons <note>Located in modern-day France, then known as Lugdunum.</note>; he was later a martyr under the Emperor Severus.

Also at this time, the version of the Bible by **Theodotion** appeared. He was a heretic and initially a disciple of Tatian <note>Tatian (c. 120–180 AD) was an Assyrian Christian writer who eventually founded a rigorous ascetic sect.</note>; later, he joined the Marcionites <term>Marcionites: Followers of Marcion, who taught that the God of the Old Testament was a different, harsher deity than the God of the New Testament.</term>. Finally, having become a Jew, he learned among them the He... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword "bræ-" suggests the word "Hebraeas" or "Hebrew language."</note>

### XIX. In the Year of Christ 195

**Aelius Pertinax** ascended to the Imperial power. He derived his surname <term>Pertinax|Meaning "persistent" or "tenacious"</term> from the fact that he accepted the command of the Empire, mandated by a Decree of the Senate <note>original: "S. C." or *Senatus Consulto*.</note>, only with great reluctance. His father ran a shop for baked goods; Pertinax himself was first a **Professor of Grammar**, and then rose through every single rank of military service. He was clearly a calm and mild man, and that same modesty with which he had accepted the Empire followed him even while he ruled.

However, while he was hurrying to restore the state of the Republic—which had been utterly ruined—to its former integrity as quickly as possible, he was murdered by his own soldiers. He had not even ruled for three full months. <note>original: "Dio." referring to the historian Cassius Dio.</note>

### XX. Didius Julianus

**Didius Julianus** reached the Imperial throne through wicked means <note>Historical sources clarify these "bad arts" as Julianus literally buying the Empire at an auction held by the Praetorian Guard.</note>; he also ruled for only a few days.

### XXI. Septimius Severus

**Septimius Severus**, an African by birth; out of favor for Pertinax, whose death he had avenged, he even wished to be called "Pertinax." He waged a civil war against **Pescennius Niger**, who was inciting rebellion in Asia, and against **Clodius Albinus**, who was doing the same in the Gallic provinces <note>Modern-day France and surrounding regions.</note>.

Regarding him, the Senate judged that he either should never have been born, or should never have died; this was because he seemed both too cruel and yet too useful to the Republic.

**Dionysius of Alexandria** <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Alexandria and student of Origen.</note> (*according to Eusebius’s Church History, Book 7, Chapter 9*) believed that those most unhappy times, predicted by **Saint John** in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> concerning the **Antichrist**, were fulfilled in the person of **Valerian**. *See Baronius, Year of Christ 259, numbers 1 and 2, and Year of Christ 260, number 2.*

### XXXVII. Marcus Aurelius Valerius Probus. 

He terrified and subdued many peoples: he recovered Gaul and defeated the Germanic Franks in several battles. *Vopiscus* <note>Flavius Vopiscus, one of the purported authors of the *Historia Augusta*</note>.

But when the Republic was pacified far and wide and flourishing everywhere, he is said to have remarked: **"In a short time, there will be no need for Legions or Garrisons."** Offended by this statement, the soldiers judged that he must be removed <note>Probus was assassinated in 282 AD by troops who resented being used for civilian labor, such as draining swamps and planting vineyards, especially after his comment suggesting their profession was becoming obsolete</note>. *Vopiscus.*

### OF UNIVERSAL HISTORY.

Indeed, there was a rush, as if in competition, into these glorious struggles; and at that time, martyrdoms <note>original: "Martyria"</note> were sought through glorious deaths much more eagerly than bishoprics <note>original: "Episcopatus"</note> are now sought after through wicked ambitions. The world was never more exhausted by any wars; nor did we ever conquer with a greater triumph than when we could not be defeated by ten years of slaughter. *See Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist who also wrote "Historical Meditations"</note>, Meditations, century 1, chapter 39 and century 3, chapter 2.*

### II.
Constantine left three sons: Constantine [II], Constantius [II], and Constans. The body of the Empire was divided among them by their father: To Constantine fell the region of the Alps, Gaul, Spain, Britain, the Orkney Islands <term>Orcades</term>, Ireland <term>Hibernia</term>, and Thule <term>Thyle</term> <note>A semi-mythical land in the far north, often identified by ancient writers as Norway, Iceland, or the Shetland Islands.</note>. ### III.
Constantius, having learned of his brother's murder, approached Italy and then Gaul with great forces; he defeated Magnentius in a massive battle.

Having escaped, however, Magnentius sent ambassadors to discuss peace, but being rejected by the victor, he fought again—and indeed unsuccessfully. Thus, fleeing to Lyon <term>Lugdunum</term>, when he saw even his own companions plotting against him and had no place to retreat, he took his own life. *Sextus Aurelius Victor. ...his own [relative], as Augustus of the West. <note>original: *Augustum Occidentis*. Certainly, Theodosius accomplished many deeds worthy of eternal praise. He restored the literary Academy <term>Gymnasium literarium; a center for higher education in the liberal arts</term> in Constantinople to a better state (*Theodosian Code, Law 3, on liberal studies*) and strictly forbade anyone from teaching publicly who had not been approved and specifically selected for this duty. Furthermore, he defined a fixed number of practitioners for each art and science: specifically, there were to be three Orators of Roman eloquence <note>Latin rhetoric</note>, ten Latin Grammarians, five Sophists of Greek eloquence, and ten Greek Grammarians, as well as one Philosopher and two Professors of Law and Statutes. By another decree (*Theodosian Code, Law 1, on professors*), he willed that those who had completed a twenty-year course of teaching should be honored with the dignity of a <term>Count of the first order; a high-ranking title in the late Roman imperial court</term>.

It is also claimed that he founded the very ancient Academy of Bologna and gifted it with the most extensive privileges. *Middendorp, On Academies, Book 4, at the beginning.* <note>While medieval legends attributed the founding of the University of Bologna to Theodosius II in 433 AD, modern historians recognize the school was established much later, in 1088. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Emperor Anastasius I's reign. The previous page detailed his rise to power and the document he signed promising to uphold the Council of Chalcedon. In the Year of Christ 492, number 81, it appears that he—rather in the manner of some modern politicians—favored syncretism <term>syncretism: the attempt to reconcile or merge different, often opposing, religious or political beliefs into a single system</term>. For when (as Evagrius <note>Evagrius Scholasticus, a 6th-century church historian</note> reports in Book 3, chapter 30) he saw that the Council of Chalcedon <note>A 451 AD council that defined Christ as having two natures; it was a major point of religious conflict</note> was accepted by some but rejected by others, and that many dissensions were arising everywhere because of it, he ordered a way to settle them. He commanded that everyone should hold whatever opinion regarding that Council was customary in the place where they lived, and furthermore, that no one should presume to debate about it. By these actions it is clearly indicated that the Emperor himself was neither an Eutychian heretic <note>original: "Eutychianum"; a follower of Eutyches, who believed Christ had only one nature, the divine</note>—since he prohibited the Council of Chalcedon from being condemned—nor was he a Catholic, since he would not permit its teachings to be preached. 

Because of this, some believe he was a follower of the Acephali <note>original: "Acephalorum"; literally "the headless ones," a group of strict Monophysites who broke away because they lacked a clear leader or "head"</note>, as is recorded in the *Acts of Theodosius the Cenobiarch* <note>Theodosius (c. 423–529) was a prominent leader of monastic life in Palestine</note>, found in the works of Surius <note>Laurentius Surius, a 16th-century historian of the lives of saints</note> for January 11th; Kedrenos and others affirm the same. But then again, others called him a Manichaean <note>a follower of a major dualistic religion that viewed the world as a struggle between light and darkness</note>, on the grounds that he was born of a Manichaean mother. Leontius <note>likely Leontius of Byzantium, a 6th-century theologian</note> likewise lists him among those heretics who, because they adhered to neither of the two mutually opposing parties, were named "the Hesitators" <note>original: "Hesitantes"</note>: these same people are found to be called "the Headless" <note>original: "Acephali"</note> because they lacked a leader. ->### SYNOPSIS ###<-

[...at which] time the Hebrew points <term>Hebrew points: vowel marks known as niqqud, added to the traditionally consonant-only Hebrew script to ensure correct pronunciation and meaning</term> were invented; see the anonymous treatise edited by Erpenius <note>Thomas Erpenius (1584–1624) was a celebrated Dutch orientalist who published several works on Hebrew and Arabic grammar</note>.

At almost this time, namely in the year of salvation 500, Clovis <note>original: "Clodouæus"</note>, King of the Franks, was the first of his line to embrace the Christian religion. He had been weary of the constant urgings of his wife, Saint Clotilde, who admonished him to embrace the Christian faith. Having procrastinated on the matter for a long time, at last, while engaged in a very fierce battle against the Alemanni <note>a confederation of Germanic tribes inhabiting the Rhine region</note>, he saw his own men rushing toward total slaughter. Pricked in his heart and with eyes raised toward heaven, he vowed to **JESUS Christ**—whom Clotilde preached as the Son of the living **GOD**—that he would receive His faith and abandon the worship of his [pagan] gods if he were granted victory over the enemies. And so, in that very instant, as the Alemanni turned their backs in flight, he gained a most glorious victory in which he killed their King and subjected the rest to his own rule. # UNIVERSAL HISTORY. 271

In the year of Christ 527, his sister’s son, **Justinian**, succeeded him. Justin, weighed down by illness and old age, had previously appointed Justinian as <term>Count of the Domestics<note>original: "Comitem domesticorum," a high-ranking military office in the late Roman Empire, originally commanding the palace guards.</note></term> and later as "Most Noble"—that is, he had created him **Caesar** <note>In this period, the title "Caesar" designated the designated heir or junior emperor.</note>. Because of his illustrious deeds both at home and abroad, he was surnamed **the Great**.

For he recovered Italy and Africa. At the beginning of his reign, he placed **Belisarius** in charge of the entire administration. Belisarius routed the vast forces of the Vandals in Africa, captured their king <note>King Gelimer, the last ruler of the Vandal Kingdom, who was defeated in 534 AD.</note>, and recovered **Carthage**. *Zonaras, volume 3; Procopius on the Vandal War.* See also *B. Gramaye on Africa, folio 55*, where it is noted that Africa later fell away because of heresies.

Procopius, in his work *On the Buildings of Justinian, Oration 6*, relates that it was certainly by Divine Providence that the Vandals had stripped all the fortresses and fortified places of Africa (except for Carthage) of their walls and defenses, so that the Africans might not have any spirit to rebel. Finding them in this state, Belisarius took possession of everything without any siege; he soon saw to it that these same places were enclosed by walls and fortified. *See the legal title in the Code regarding the office of the Praetorian Prefect of Africa.*

When the Vandalic War was finished, Belisarius set out for Italy, where he occupied Naples and routed the Goths.

Afterwards he <note>Belisarius</note> came to Rome, where he was received lovingly and honorably by everyone. Departing from there, he occupied towns and fortifications everywhere, including **Perugia**, and later besieged **Ravenna**. There **Vitiges**, King of the Goths, having encountered him and lost his army, was captured and led to **Constantinople** by Belisarius. *Diaconus, book 16; Jordanes, book 1; Blondus, decade 1, book 5.*

He was succeeded by one and then another, and finally by **Totila**. In the absence of Belisarius, Totila raged throughout all of Italy; he besieged **Rome**, captured it, plundered it, and set it on fire. *Procopius, book 3 on the Gothic War; Evagrius, book 4, chapter 20.*

Therefore, Belisarius was recalled. Having finished the war against the **Parthians** <note>The author uses "Parthians" to refer to the Sassanid Persians, a common archaism in Renaissance historical texts.</note>, who were again laying waste to **Syria**, he returned to Italy and restored the nearly deserted city <note>Rome</note>. From there, having encountered the enemy, he fought successfully. However, while he was sailing to **Sicily** for the sake of the grain supply, he was recalled by **Justinian**. This event indeed provided the opportunity for Totila to return to Rome with his strength restored. Totila is called **Badiula**, or rather **Dadiula**, by **Jordanes**.

The Emperor <note>original: "Cæsar"; referring here to Justinian I</note> then put **Narses the Eunuch** in charge of the Italian war. It was Narses who finally drove the **Goths** out of all Italy; this task was made easier because the Goths had lost their King, **Totila**, who had died from a wound. *Pomponius Laetus.*

**Belisarius**, however, was of the German nation <note>While the author identifies him as German, modern historians typically place Belisarius’s birthplace in Thrace, in the modern-day Balkans.</note>, and he was so dear to the Prince **Justinian** that the Emperor ordered coins to be struck showing himself on one side and Belisarius in armor on the other, with this inscription: *Belisarius, the hope and glory of the Romans.* Yet, he eventually fell from his master's favor—so much so that some write he was blinded, and others that he was reduced to extreme poverty. *See Baronius for the Year of Christ 561; Sleidan on the Four Monarchies, and the commentary there by Meibom, page 269; and my own work, "On Political Counsel," chapter 4, number 107.*

**Procopius**, in the beginning of his *Secret History*, reports that Belisarius was defiled by various vices and was made infamous by the unchastity of his wife <note>His wife was Antonina, a close friend of Empress Theodora; Procopius's *Secret History* is a famous "tell-all" memoir that stands in stark contrast to his official, praising histories.</note>. *On this matter, the notes of Alemannus should be consulted thoroughly.* **Albert of Stade** also records that he was German, on page 56.

Furthermore, Justinian collected the **Laws** which are still used today in academic schools and legal courts. ### SYNOPSIS

Relying on his promises, Empress Theodora <note>The influential wife of Emperor Justinian I</note> wrote to General Belisarius <note>A famous Byzantine general who reclaimed much of the Western Roman Empire</note>, instructing him to find some cause—or even to invent one—to depose Pope Silverius. Likewise, when the doctrine of Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) whose complex views on the soul and salvation were later deemed heretical</note>—concerning the existence of souls before they enter bodies and the eventual end of the punishments of hell—was being revived in Palestine, Origen was condemned once again. However, Theodore, the Bishop of Caesarea, who was a follower of Origen, was provoked by this condemnation. He argued that if it were permissible to condemn the teachings of authors who were already dead, then Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and Ibas <note>Ibas of Edessa</note> should also be condemned. These men had written things contrary to the Council of Chalcedon <note>A landmark meeting of bishops in 451 AD that defined the nature of Christ</note>, and yet they had not been condemned there. On this occasion, the controversy of the **Three Chapters** <term>The Three Chapters (Tria Capitula) refers to a series of specific writings by three 5th-century bishops that became the center of a major theological and political conflict</term> arose, over which the Doctors of the Church subsequently fought in great conflict. When Emperor Justinian—perhaps incautiously—condemned those aforementioned "chapters," many evils arose, and the Church itself was harassed by a dreadful and long-lasting schism <note>A formal split or division within the Church</note>. *Baronius, in the Year of Christ 538, number 7, and throughout.*

On this occasion, the **Fifth Ecumenical Synod**, as it is called, was celebrated in Constantinople in the Year of Christ 553. *Longus <note>Original: "Longus fol. 172." Reference to the historian François Longue de la Cointe.</note> folio 172, etc.*

Also during the reign of Justinian, years began to be numbered not by Olympiads <note>Four-year periods used by the ancient Greeks</note>, or by Consuls, or by Indictions <term>Indictions: A 15-year tax cycle used for dating documents in the Roman and Byzantine Empires</term>, but from the Incarnation of our Lord Christ. This was done so that, as Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 673–735 AD), an English monk and historian</note> says in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45, the beginning of our hope might become better known, and the cause of human restoration—namely the Passion of our Redeemer—might shine forth more clearly. This was achieved through the work of **Dionysius Exiguus** <note>Dionysius "the Humble" (c. 470–544 AD), the monk who invented the AD/BC dating system</note>, who composed the Paschal Cycle <term>Paschal Cycle: A mathematical system used to determine the date of Easter over a long period</term>. *Marianus Scotus <note>An 11th-century Irish chronicler</note>; and whom Cassiodorus mentions in "On Divine Learning," chapter 23; see also Albert of Stade, folio 57.* However, Sethus Calvisius <note>A German astronomer and scholar of chronology (1556–1615)</note> strives to prove in the prologue of his *Chronology*, chapter 47, that there is a two-year discrepancy between the true year of the Birth of Christ and the Christian Era established by Dionysius Exiguus. Add to this the illustrious Master **Kepler** <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the world-renowned astronomer and mathematician</note>, my kinsman and former teacher, in his *Chronological Forest*, or his consideration of the opinion of Laurentius Susliga, a Pole, who argued for a four-year difference in this unusual Epoch.

<header>UNIVERSAL HISTORY</header>

In the year of **Christ 565**, [Justin II] <note>Though the text does not name him here, Justin II succeeded Justinian I in 565 AD</note> inherited an Imperial state in a precarious condition, as the Catholic faith had been somewhat unsettled by his predecessor. He did indeed compose an edict concerning the true faith, which **Evagrius** <note>Evagrius Scholasticus (c. 536–594 AD), a Syrian scholar and historian of the Christian Church</note> records in *Book 5, Chapter 4*; however, he was a prince of a sluggish disposition. He defiled the praiseworthy deeds he performed at the very beginning of his reign with greed and a shameful lifestyle. *Baronius, Year of Christ 566, number 3.*

Jealous also of the glory of **Narses** <note>Narses (c. 478–573 AD) was one of the Great Byzantine generals who re-conquered Italy from the Goths</note>, he removed this man—renowned for his skills in both war and peace—from the administration of Italy. Narses was incensed by this atrocious injury from the Emperor, as well as by the insult of the Empress **Sophia**, who called the eunuch back to his spinning task <note>Original: *ad pensum reuocantis*. Referring to the legendary insult where the Empress told the eunuch Narses to return to the women's quarters to spin wool</note>. This insult turned his anger into a localized rage. He is said to have threatened the Empress, claiming he would weave such a web that neither she nor her husband could ever unravel it. *Paul the Deacon, "On the Deeds of the Lombards," Book 1, Chapter 5; but see Baronius, Year of Christ 567, number 2; and Sethus Calvisius <note>Sethus Calvisius (1556–1615), a German astronomer and chronologer</note> under the same year.*

Consequently, he summoned the **Lombards** <note>Original: *Longobardos*</note>—a people originating from Scandinavia <note>Original: *Scandia*</note> whose brave and faithful service he had used to drive the Goths out of Italy—to move from Pannonia <note>A region in central Europe, including parts of modern-day Hungary and Austria</note> into Italy. For more on the Lombards and how they secured their empire, see Camerarius <note>Philipp Camerarius (1537–1624), a German scholar</note>, *Historical Meditations, Century 2, Chapter 49*; also Sigonius <note>Carlo Sigonio (1524–1584), an Italian historian known for his work on the Middle Ages</note> in his book *On the Kingdom of Italy*, as well as Warnefrid and Paul the Deacon.

These people <note>The Lombards</note>, having left Pannonia <note>An ancient Roman province in Central Europe, primarily modern-day Hungary</note> to their Hun allies, followed King **Alboin** <note>King of the Lombards from c. 560 to 572 AD; he led his people into Italy</note> and occupied **Cisalpine Gaul** <note>Northern Italy</note> in their first military surge. From them, the region was first called Longobardia; later, by a corruption of the word, it was called **Lombardy**. Alboin established the seat of his kingdom at **Ticinum**, the city which was later called **Pavia**.

Shortly before the arrival of the Lombards in Italy, it is recorded that terrifying nocturnal omens and fiery battle lines were seen in the sky, flashing with the human blood that was later to be shed. **Saint Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory I, also known as Gregory the Great (reigned 590–604 AD)</note> in his *first homily on the Gospel*, and after him **Paul the Deacon** <note>A Benedictine monk and historian of the Lombards (c. 720–799 AD)</note> in *Book 1, Chapter 5*, are the sources for this. Certainly, the aforementioned St. Gregory counts the Lombard raids among the other most cruel persecutions of the Church (*Letter 34 of Book 4; Dialogues, Book 3, Chapters 11, 26, etc.*). Furthermore, **Procopius** <note>A prominent Byzantine historian (c. 500–565 AD)</note> clearly indicates in *Book 2 of the Gothic War* that the Lombards were Christians. However, it is evident from the same Gregory the Great (*Homily 1 on the Gospel; Dialogues, Book 3, Chapter 26, etc.; also Chapter 37*) that many still persisted as Pagans <note>Original: *Gentiles*</note>, and those who were Christians belonged to the **Arian** sect <note>Arianism was a Christian movement that held that Jesus was not co-eternal with God the Father; it was considered a heresy by the Roman Catholic Church</note>.

This **Justin** <note>Emperor Justin II</note> is written to have established a new magistrate throughout Italy: the **Exarch** <note>The Exarch of Ravenna was the Byzantine Emperor's primary representative and military governor in Italy</note>.

*Flavio Biondo, Decade 1, Book 6.* But Sethus Calvisius <note>A famous German chronologist and astronomer (1556–1615).</note> dates the birth of Muhammad <note>original: "Machomeri"</note> to the year of Christ 570.
   Likewise, under the Emperor Maurice, a contention concerning primacy <note>The claim of supreme authority over the whole Church.</note> flourished between the Roman Popes Pelagius II and even Gregory the Great, and John, the Bishop of Constantinople. *Baronius, Year of Christ 595.* For John called himself the "Universal Patriarch."    Around those times, Reccared, King of the Visigoths in Spain, having abandoned Arianism <note>A branch of Christianity that believed Jesus was created by God the Father and was not equal to Him; it was considered a heresy by the Roman Church.</note>, joined the orthodox Church. *Isidore of Seville, in the Chronicle of the Goths.*
   Similarly, Agilulf, King of the Lombards, together with all the Lombards who had been entangled in the impieties of Paganism or Arianism, was converted to the Catholic faith and was named Paul in his baptism. *Paul the Deacon, Book 3, Chapter 14 and the last, and Book 4, Chapters 1 and 2.* Although later Arioald and other kings were most tenacious in their Arian impiety; and also, in almost every city, there were at times two bishops: one Catholic and the other Arian. *Paul the Deacon, Book 4, Chapter 44.*

## XXV. Justinian II
**Justinian II** <note>The text refers to him as "Heraclius Iustinianus," but he is historically known as Justinian II, the last emperor of the Heraclian dynasty.</note> in the Year of Christ 682, or as others prefer, 686. As the heir to the Empire, he managed the State poorly due to his youth and inexperience. For he was a youth of sixteen years, a man of weak character, and therefore possessed no wisdom. *Cedrenus.* <note>George Kedrenos, a 11th-century Byzantine historian.</note>

Puffed up by his **Slavic Legions**, <note>Reference to the Slavic tribes settled in Asia Minor whom Justinian recruited into the army.</note> and having wrongly broken a treaty, he brought war upon the **Arabs**. But they, having invoked God as a witness to the treaty and carrying the actual tablets of the treaty suspended from a spear, met the Emperor in battle. Once the Slavic troops began to flee at the start of the engagement, the Arabs inflicted a massive slaughter. *Paul the Deacon, book 9. Tursellinus:* Therefore, whether because of the magnitude of this disaster or on account of his cruelty, he became hated by the City. He was seized by **General Leontius**, whom he had previously held in chains. Having had his nose mutilated—from which the nickname **Rhinotmetos** <note>Greek for "the slit-nosed."</note> was given to him—he was exiled to **Chersonesus**. <note>An ancient colony on the Crimean Peninsula.</note> Furthermore, **Theodore the False-Monk** and **Stephen the Treasurer**, by whose service he had harassed the people in dreadful ways, were dragged into the public forum with ropes tied to their feet and burned. *Cedrenus and Zonaras.*

XXVI. Philippicus Bardanes <note>Byzantine Emperor from 711 to 713 AD.</note>, to whom, as has already been said, the army had defected, began to rule in the Year of Christ 712. He immediately attempted to abolish the Sixth Synod <note>The Third Council of Constantinople (680–681), which concluded that Jesus Christ had two wills (human and divine) corresponding to his two natures.</note>, which had condemned the Monothelite heresy <note>A theological position that claimed Christ had only one "will." He was moved to fulfill this with all the greater zeal because the person who had predicted his rise to the Empire had also added this as if it were a Divine Oracle: that his reign would be long-lasting if he acted upon this without delay. *Kedrenos and Theophanes.* <note>George Kedrenos and Theophanes the Confessor were major Byzantine chroniclers whose works are primary sources for this period.</note>

For that reason, he was pronounced a schismatic <note>A person who promotes a split or division within the Church.</note> by Pope Constantine of Rome. *Anastasius, in his Life of Constantine.* <note>Referring to the *Liber Pontificalis*, a record of early popes often attributed to Anastasius the Librarian.</note> And contrary to what I said had been promised to him by the oracle, he did not hold the Empire for a full year and a half; after a great banquet provided to the more noble citizens, while he was resting at midday, he was captured by certain Patricians <note>High-ranking nobles or officials.</note>, blinded <note>original: *exoculatus*. In Byzantine culture, blinding a deposed ruler was a common way to ensure they could never again hold the throne, as the Emperor was required to be physically unblemished.</note>, and cast into exile. *Paul the Deacon, Book 6, Chapter 34.*

On the following day, after the whole populace had been called together in the Great Church <note>The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.</note>, Artemius was crowned—who had been the private secretary to the same Philippicus—and he was called Anastasius, the second of that name.

### UNIVERSAL HISTORY
<page-num>307</page-num>

<margin>*Baronius, Year of Christ 716, number 1.* <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607) was a cardinal and historian; his *Annales Ecclesiastici* is a primary source for church history.</note></margin>
In the midst of these events, while the fleet of the **Saracens** <note>A term commonly used in historical texts to refer to Arab or Muslim forces.</note> was hurrying from **Alexandria** toward **Phoenicia** to cut cypress wood for the construction of ships, Emperor **Anastasius** <note>Anastasius II, who reigned from 713 to 715 AD.</note> sent a fleet to oppose them. However, a mutiny arose among the soldiers at **Rhodes**. The faction that gained the upper hand—fearing the Emperor's retribution for their rebellion—retreated toward their own lands and arrived at **Adramyttium**, a coastal city of **Aeolis** <note>A region on the western coast of modern-day Turkey.</note>. There, they found a local man of humble birth named **Theodosius**, who served as a collector of public taxes. Despite his reluctance and his attempts to find a hiding place, they forced him to take the title of Emperor. After a six-month siege of **Constantinople**, he was admitted into the city through treachery; he then compelled the Emperor **Anastasius** to take holy orders and confined him to a monastery.

<margin>*Zonaras, Kedrenos.* <note>Joannes Zonaras and George Kedrenos were influential Byzantine chroniclers and historians.</note></margin>
But not much later, **Theodosius**, who desired a quiet life rather than the burdens of ruling, surrendered the Empire to **Leo the Isaurian**, the Prefect of the forces (also known by the name **Conon**), in the Year of Christ 717.

It is recorded that **Theodosius**, having become a member of the clergy along with his son, died at **Ephesus**. It is said that while he lived, he devoted himself excellently to philosophy, and after his death, he was even renowned for performing miracles.

A little while before, Petronax, a citizen of Brescia <note>original: Brixianus</note>, came to Rome and, at the encouragement of Pope Gregory, restored Monte Cassino <note>Cassinum</note>, the Benedictine monastery which had been in ruins for nearly 140 years. XXVII. During the reign of Leo <note>Emperor Leo III, known as the Isaurian</note>, the Saracens besieged Constantinople for three years by land and sea; but at length, nearly destroyed by a plague, they were forced to return home. *Diaconus, book 6, chapter 47. Baronius, Year of Christ 717, number 3 and following.*

And this man <note>Emperor Leo</note> cast out all statues and images of the saints from the churches <note>original: Templis</note>; for this reason, he was in bad odor with the Roman Pontiff and the Western Church. Because of this, he was called an <term>Iconomachus</term> <note>Image-fighter; from the Greek 'eikon' (image) and 'mache' (battle)</note> by them, and they say the dogma of the <term>Iconoclasts</term> <note>Image-breakers; those who destroy religious icons</note> arose from him. Baronius <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius, an influential 16th-century historian</note> attributes the origin of this movement to certain Jewish impostors, to whom Leo had bound himself by an oath—in reward for their prediction that he would become Emperor—to do whatever they might demand. And although many Emperors had been heretics, Baronius writes that never until this time had it happened that any, besides this man, was a <term>heresiarch</term> <note>a founder or leader of a heretical sect</note>.

XXVIII. After Leo, his son Constantine began his rule in the year of Christ 741.
