### CHAPTER XVII.
# CONCERNING THE EMPERORS
## *of the Franks.*

The Roman Caesars ruling in the East, because they were quite far away—having held the seat of Empire in Constantinople <note>original: "Constantinopoli"</note> since the time of Constantine the Great <note>original: "Constantini Magni"</note>—and because they were not only continuously agitated by foreign wars but also hindered by domestic and civil disputes, almost entirely neglected Italy. At the very least, they were unable to defend it properly, especially with the Lombards <note>original: "Longobardis"; a Germanic people who had settled in Italy and were frequently at odds with the Papacy</note> rampaging there. Furthermore, most of these Eastern rulers also disagreed sharply with the Roman Bishops <note>original: "Romanis Episcopis"; the Popes</note>; out of a certain animosity toward them, the Emperors were not particularly moved by the successes of the Lombards and refused to settle the various difficulties and uprisings. For this reason, the Popes looked around for external protection. Because at that time there was no family more illustrious or powerful than that of the Kings of France <note>original: "Franciae Regum"; the Frankish Carolingian dynasty</note>, owing to the greatness of their achievements, the Popes fled to them as if to a harbor in turbulent times.

And while in Constantinople, under the rule of Constantine <note>original: "Constantino"; Constantine VI</note> and Irene <note>Empress Irene of Athens</note>, there was such tumul—

# S Y N O P S I S

->Events were conducted with great vigor;<- the fame of Charles, King of the Franks <note>better known to history as Charlemagne</note>, was celebrated, and his power was no less impressive. Regarding him, see *Sigonius’s Kings of Italy, the Bavarian Annals by the Reverend Father Brunner (part 2), the Anonymous Saxon Poet, Eginhard in Reuber’s collection, Hector of Aachen, and the Annals edited by Pithou.* 

For after the war in Aquitaine was completed, having been requested by Hadrian, the Roman Pontiff <note>Pope Hadrian I, who reigned from 772–795 AD</note>, he came into Italy with an army. Just as his father, Pepin, had crushed Aistulf, the King of the Lombards; so too did Charles capture Aistulf's successor, Desiderius, who had been a heavy burden to Italy and Hadrian. After a long siege of Pavia, Charles took him prisoner, cast down his son Adalgis from the throne, and expelled him from all of Italy. In this way, he gained possession of the entire Kingdom of the Lombards. *See Regino (book 3), Guagninus (book 4, chapter 1), and Aemilius of Verona’s History of the Franks (book 2).*

Furthermore, Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle* that once Pavia was captured, Charles returned to Rome. In a Synod of 153 bishops <note>original: "Antistitum"</note> celebrated by Pope Hadrian, the right of choosing the Roman Pontiff <note>original: "jus eligendi Romanum Pontificem"</note> was granted to him. It was also established that Archbishops and Bishops throughout the individual provinces were to receive <term>investitures</term> <note>investiture: the formal ceremony where a ruler grants a bishop the symbols of their spiritual and temporal power, such as a staff or ring</note> from him. *See Chapter "Hadrian," distinction 65, and the works of Lord Goldast.*

There, after several days, an investigation was conducted regarding the crimes that had been alleged against Pope Leo <note>Pope Leo III, whose papacy was marked by conflict with the Roman nobility</note> by his enemies. Having called upon the name of the Most Holy Trinity, he cleared himself of those accusations by a solemn oath. *Baronius, Year of Christ 800.*

The rebellious Roman citizens—some of whom were leaders of the city and who had treated the Pope quite poorly—numbering three hundred in total, were ordered by Charles to be beheaded on a single day in the Lateran Field <note>original: "Campo Lateranensi," the area surrounding the Lateran Palace in Rome</note>. ### SYNOPSIS

On Christmas Day (in the Year of Christ 800, in the Basilica of Saint Peter, with the entire Clergy, the People, and the Nobles <note>original: "Optimatibus"</note> gathered), while Charles was rising from prayer, Pope Leo, with his own hands, placed the Imperial Crown upon his head and proclaimed him Emperor of the Romans. Then all those standing by acclaimed him three times with one voice: *To Charles, the Most Pious Augustus, crowned by God, Great and Peaceful Emperor of the Romans, Life and Victory!* <note>original: "Carolo Pijssimo Augusto, à Deo coronato Magno, Pacifico, Imperatori Romanorum, Vita & Victoria"</note> And soon after, the same Pope anointed him with holy oil.

Einhard <note>Einhard (c. 775–840) was a dedicated servant of Charlemagne and his primary biographer</note>, however—or Eginhard—who was present, when writing in the *Life of Charlemagne* about this same coronation, asserts that it was carried out without Charles’s prior knowledge; indeed, he claims that Charles took it poorly when it happened <note>Einhard famously wrote that Charles would not have entered the church that day, even though it was a great feast, if he had known the Pope's intention</note>. However, whether a transfer of power <note>original: "translatio," referring to the "Translatio Imperii" or the transfer of the Roman Empire from the Greeks in the East to the Franks in the West</note> of this kind was done justly and by the authority of the Pope, or rather by the decree of the Roman People, requires a deeper investigation than can be undertaken here. See the individual treatises on this matter by Flacius Illyricus <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer and historian</note>, Franciscus Junius, Henning Arnisaeus, and Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation</note>, as well as Baronius for the Year of Christ 800, and Gretser, volume 2, in defense of Bellarmine.

Charles was indeed the first of all the Germans to be elevated to the Imperial dignity. Jean Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher</note>, in chapter 7, is incorrect on this point.

This time, however, he had summoned the Huns (whom others called the Avars <note>Medieval chroniclers often used the names 'Huns' and 'Avars' interchangeably for the nomadic people settled in the Danube basin</note>) to his aid. He instead allowed Tassilo to enter a monastery along with his son, Theodo. 

As for the Huns who had been enticed by Tassilo, they organized two armies: one attacked the March of Friuli <note>original: "Marcam Forojuliensem," a frontier territory in northeastern Italy</note> and the other attacked Bavaria. However, they were defeated in both locations and fled back to their own territories in Pannonia <note>A region centered in modern-day Hungary</note>. They did not remain quiet, but renewed the war for the next eight consecutive years. They suffered massive casualties, leading almost to the total annihilation of their people. The Franks were enriched in an extraordinary way by the spoils taken from them—treasures which had been amassed from the ruins of many other nations. Until that time, the Franks had seemed almost impoverished by comparison. *Einhard; Ado of Vienne.* <note>Einhard was Charlemagne's biographer; Ado was a 9th-century chronicler and Archbishop of Vienne.</note>

When in the year of Christ 933, the Hungarians <note>The Magyars, whose raids across Europe were a defining threat of the 10th century</note> had spent the winter in Eastern Germany through wickedness and all manner of outrages, they divided themselves into two armies. ...that he, the Emperor himself, arriving in Rome with his army, was received by the citizens after the Pope had fled. From these citizens, a promise of loyalty was secured, and they swore that they would never elect or ordain a Pope without the consent and choice of Emperor Otto himself and his son, King Otto.

After this promise was made, at the request of the bishops and the common people, the Emperor presided over a Council in Rome at St. Peter’s in the month of November. This council was attended by the bishops of Italy, several from Germany, as well as the entire Clergy and the leaders of the City. During these proceedings, various and atrocious crimes were charged against John <note>John XII, who had originally crowned Otto but then turned against him.</note>, including murder, perjury, sacrilege, incest, and other unspeakable wickednesses. When John was summoned by the Synod <note>original: "Synodo." A formal meeting of church leaders to decide on matters of doctrine or discipline.</note> to appear and clear himself of these charges, he wrote back nothing except that he was excommunicating all the bishops if they presumed to elect any other Pope. Nevertheless, with the Emperor granting their petition, they appointed another in his place and consecrated, with the customary rites, Leo—the Chief Secretary <note>original: "Protoscriniarium." A high-ranking administrative official in the papal court.</note> of that same Church—as the eighth Pope of that name. This matter remains a subject of various debates among historians. *See Baronius, in the Year of Christ 963; Gretser, Apology, chapter 17; Longus, folio 289, etc.* <note>These refer to Cesare Baronius, the Jesuit theologian Jacob Gretser (1562–1625), and likely the historian François Longueval.</note>

And certainly, throughout his long reign, he was a rare example of human happiness; for indeed, he ruled with a constant spirit of virtue and glory for thirty years. *See Brouwer, folio 122, where he discusses his piety.*

### VI. Henry the Second

**Henry the Second**, Duke of Bavaria and a relative of Emperor **Otto the Great**, began his Imperial rule in the **Year of Christ 1025**; <note>Historical records typically date the start of Henry II’s reign to 1002 and his Imperial coronation to 1014; he died in 1024. He was especially favored by the clergy because he conferred so many benefits upon them. His devotion to sacred things and holy persons was so great that when **Saint Ramuold**, the Abbot of St. Emmeram, died at Regensburg in the fifth year after the death of Emperor Otto, this same King placed his own shoulder under the **bier** <note>original: "feretro"; a stand on which a corpse or coffin is placed.</note> to carry it. <note>Baronius, Year of Christ 1007, number 1.</note>

The King <note>original: "Caesar"</note>, however, being by nature prone to vices, began to live a wild life. For although the supreme power was primarily in the hands of the Archbishop of Mainz and the Archbishop of Cologne, they frequently called upon Adalbert, the Archbishop of Bremen. *See Albert of Stade.*

Adalbert was wonderfully favored by the youth. In order to possess the boy’s loyalty exclusively, he yielded to Henry’s feelings and will in all things. Above all, he was the leader and instigator in allowing Henry to indulge in wandering and strictly forbidden lusts. Upon returning to Germany, Henry gathered his forces. Rudolf, who relied primarily on the support of the Saxons, did the same. In their third conflict, Rudolf was severely wounded and died shortly thereafter.

You see now what end has befallen us, for in the hand with which I violated my oaths, I have received this mortal wound. Let those who incited us to this action see to it how they have led us, lest perhaps we have been led to the precipice of eternal damnation. <note>original: "Videtis manum dextram meam... ne fortè deducti simus in præcipitium æternæ damnationis."</note>

# OF UNIVERSAL HISTORY

**Lambert of Hersfeld** <note>original: "Lambertus Schaffnaburgensis"; an important 11th-century German chronicler</note> seems to be susceptible to biases <note>original: "affectibus"; referring to emotional or political prejudices</note>. Our city of **Tübingen** first published his work in the Year of Christ 1525, under a truncated and, at that time, still unknown name. One may also consult **Guilliman** <note>Charles Guillimann (1568–1633), a Swiss historian noted for his work on the Habsburgs</note> in Book 5 of *Habsburg*, page 158, etc.

Around the Year of Christ 1086, a certain professor who had died at **Paris** <note>original: "Lutetiæ"; the Roman name for Paris</note>, when he was just about to be buried, is said to have suddenly cried out: *I have been damned by a just judgment.* He did this a second and then a third time. While all those standing by were struck with terror, they say a certain professor named **Bruno** <note>Saint Bruno of Cologne (c. 1030–1101), the founder of the Carthusian Order</note> said: "Let us leave the world, lest we perish in like manner." 

And with a few others, he reached the forest called **Chartreuse** <note>original: "Carthusiam"; a mountain range in the French Alps</note>. There he established small cells and an order of Monks, who were called **Carthusians** after the name of the place. Perpetual silence was required of them; they wore an inner garment of hair-cloth <note>original: "cilicina"; a rough shirt made of goat hair worn as a form of penance</note> and a black outer cloak, and they never ate meat. (See the *Magdeburg Centuries* <note>original: "Cent. Magd."; a monumental 16th-century history of the Church written from a Lutheran perspective</note>). Furthermore, the primary rule for the life of the Carthusian Monks was written down by **Peter, Abbot of Cluny** <note>Peter the Venerable (c. 1092–1156), a famous medieval abbot and theologian</note>. **Pope Urban II** summoned Bruno to him from his solitude and kept him for three years against his will, utilizing his labor in the convening of Church Councils. (See **Baronius** <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Catholic cardinal and historian who wrote the *Annales Ecclesiastici*</note> for the Year of Christ 1092, number 2.)

### SYNOPSIS

Shortly after, specifically in the Year of Christ 1098, the **Cistercian** order began <note>original: "Cistertiensium ordo"</note> through **Abbot Robert** <note>Saint Robert of Molesme (c. 1028–1111), one of the founders of the Cistercian Order</note> and other monks who departed from **Molesme** <note>original: "Molismo"; a Benedictine abbey in Burgundy</note>. Also flourishing under this Emperor <note>Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor</note> was **Ivo, Bishop of Chartres** <note>original: "Iuo Episcopus Carnotensis"; a significant figure in the development of canon law</note>, who compiled **Decretals** <note>original: "Decretalia"; collections of papal letters or rulings on church law</note> from the Canons of the Saints. These were in use before the *Decree of Gratian* <note>original: "Decretum Gratiani"; the standard collection of canon law in the Middle Ages, compiled around 1140</note>. *Trithemius.* He is considered the patron of legal scholars.

Likewise, **Marianus Scotus**, a monk of **Fulda**; **William of Malmesbury**, an Englishman; **Conrad of Liechtenaw**, the Abbot of **Ursperg**; and others were also famous at this time.

Similarly, under this Emperor, **Jerusalem** was captured and seized from the **Saracens** <note>a medieval term used by Europeans to describe Muslim peoples</note>. **William, Archbishop of Tyre**, as well as the author of the *Jerusalem Chronicle* (published by **Reiner Reineccius**), provide a lengthy account of the history of this war.

For indeed, Pope **Urban II**, having held a Council in **France** <note>the Council of Clermont in 1095, which initiated the First Crusade</note>, ignited the Christian Princes toward the war for Jerusalem. In the Year of Christ 1112, after the Emperor had returned to Germany, the Pope summoned a Council in Rome at the **Lateran** <note>The Lateran Palace and Basilica, the ancient and primary seat of the Popes</note>, which many Archbishops and Bishops attended. It is also related that at that time the <term>Civil Law|Ius Ciuile: The Roman legal system codified by Justinian</term>, which had been compiled long before by the command of the Emperor Justinian but suppressed by the storms of wars, was brought back into the light. *Aventinus, book 6; Sigonius, "On the Kingdom of Italy," book 11; Ursberg; Lehman, book 5, chapter 46.*

For in the war waged against Roger, at Amalfi <note>The text reads "Melfis," likely referring to the capture of the "Pandects" during the siege of Amalfi in 1135</note> in Apulia, he found the **Roman Laws**, which he gave to the people of Pisa and ordered that they be explained and that the law in the Roman Empire be pronounced according to them. These books were later transferred to Florence into the Medici Library, where they still exist today. From this, they are called the **Florentine Pandects** <term>Pandectae: Also known as the Digest, a massive compendium of Roman legal opinions</term>.

Certainly the Barbarians wished to destroy the **Roman Laws** along with the name and greatness of the Roman Empire, and in the meantime to supplant and impose their own laws.

# UNIVERSAL HISTORY. 417

After the profession of Law had lain hidden in Italy for nearly five hundred years, it was recalled and brought into the light once more by the singular counsel of God.

In particular, Werner (commonly called Irnerius), a German man in Italy who at that time possessed great influence and authority, earned more merit than others regarding this <term>Civil Law|Ius Ciuile: The body of Roman law, specifically the Corpus Juris Civilis, which forms the basis for many modern legal systems</term>, which in the judgment of all wise men contains the most abundant wisdom. For he recalled the books of Civil Law, which were then completely unknown; he was the advisor and persuader to Lothair <note>Lothair III, Holy Roman Emperor (reigned 1125–1137)</note> that they should be presented in schools. He himself was also the first to reopen the profession of Law in Italy, where it had collapsed and become extinct—*as Valentin Forster relates in his History of Law.*

From the school of Irnerius, many most learned men emerged; and the study of Law began to grow and offer itself up, not so much because of the crowd of students, but because of the multitude of teachers; for new things almost always draw and entice minds to themselves. But among the rest, Placentinus <note>A famous 12th-century legal scholar who founded the law school at Montpellier</note> achieved particular fame in those times, being the first to propagate the profession of Law into France <note>original: "Galliam"</note> *—Forster, in the same place.*

His piety is praised by Catholics because, while stationed on military expeditions, he was accustomed to hear a Mass for the deceased at the very first light of dawn, then a second for the army, and finally a third for the day. Furthermore, alongside his August Spouse <note>Empress Richenza of Northeim</note>, he would wash the feet of widows and orphans, dry them with his hair, and kiss them, distributing food and drink to them generously. He prioritized relieving the complaints and oppressions of the Churches, placing the affairs of the Empire in the final position of importance. He was never torn away from the company of Bishops and Abbots; he honored Priests as fathers, cherished the poor as sons, and widows as mothers. He was ever-vigilant in prayer and offered frequent tears from a contrite heart to God. *Following Peter of Cassino <note>Peter the Deacon, librarian of Monte Cassino</note>, [as cited by] Baronius <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius, author of the Annales Ecclesiastici</note>. # UNIVERSAL HISTORY #

At the beginning of his reign, after Germany had been pacified, he entered Italy with a great army. He punished the people of Verona, by whom he had been treated with contempt, and as an example, he broke the necks of several of the leaders with a noose <note>A reference to execution by hanging</note>. Having set out for Rome, he was consecrated by Adrian III <note>The text says Adrian III, but this is likely a chronological error by the author or printer for Adrian IV, the only English Pope, who crowned Frederick in 1155</note>, and he suppressed the rioting citizens. Indeed, the Roman Arnoldists <note>Followers of Arnold of Brescia, a radical reformer who called for the Church to renounce political power and property</note>, upon hearing of the King’s arrival, sent a delegation of their Senators to him in an attempt to forestall his actions and win him over with soft words. However, they were rebuked by him, and their efforts proved to be in vain. *Baronius, Year of Christ 1155, number 5; Albert of Stade, folio 189, etc.*

While the Emperor was returning to Germany, the Milanese acted with great arrogance toward their neighbors and began to rebuild Tortona, which had been destroyed by the Caesar <note>A title used here for the Emperor Frederick</note>. Therefore, returning with a massive army, he conquered Milan, aided by the people of Crema <note>original: "Cremensibus"</note> and others. Once the city was captured, the multitude of common people was spared through the intercession of the German Princes. *Rahewin <note>original: "Radenicus," the chronicler who continued the work of Otto of Freising</note>, book 1, chapter 32, etc. But later, for a third...*

# SYNOPSIS #

...his singular opinion, and because he persisted in obstinately defending it, his stubbornness passed into a common proverb among legal scholars <note>original: "Iurisconsultos"</note> even to this day; they call him a *Martinus* who clings with stubborn zeal to his own singular opinion. *See Baronius, Year of Christ 1158, number 2 and following; Lehman, book 5, chapter 59.*

Upon the death of **Hadrian** <note>Pope Hadrian IV, the only English pope</note> in the year of Christ 1159, two Popes contended for the leadership of the Church: **Alexander III** and **Victor** <note>Victor IV, an antipope supported by the Emperor</note>. The Emperor leaned more toward Victor. He called a Council at **Pavia**, where, after **Alexander** was condemned, **Victor** was approved. *Baronius, Year of Christ 1159, number 7, etc., and Year of Christ 1160; see also Albert of Stade, folio 190b and 192b.*

XVI. Otto IV, Duke of Saxony, in the Year of Christ 1208, called an assembly at Frankfurt, where he was elected Emperor by fifty Princes who had gathered. He immediately outlaws Otto of Wittelsbach <note>Otto of Wittelsbach was the man who had assassinated the previous claimant, Philip of Swabia</note>. Six Princes—three from the sacred order: the Archbishops of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne; and just as many secular princes: the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the Duke of Saxony (who at that time was of Brunswick), and the Margrave of Brandenburg—shall elect him. If these should be in disagreement, they shall choose the King of Bohemia to join them.”* Calvisius, Year of Christ 1208.

It is reported that *Pope Gregory*, <note>original: "Gregorius Pontifex"; referring to Pope Gregory X, who reigned from 1271 to 1276.</note> having sent a Legate, commanded the *Electors*—the *clergy* indeed under penalty of being deprived of their office, but the *secular Princes* under penalty of excommunication—that, putting aside all delay, they should designate a *Protector of the Church and Roman Emperor*. Through the intervention of Alfonso's Legates, nothing was achieved; the previous goodwill with which they had embraced *Alfonso* had changed into public resentment. They held *Ottokar's* stubborn pride in contempt, because he had previously rejected the *Kingdom of the Romans* offered to him by the *Archbishop of Cologne*, preferring his *Principality of Bohemia*. After three days were spent in deliberation, with their votes hurried, this *Rudolph* <note>Rudolph I of Habsburg (reigned 1273–1291), whose election ended the period of instability known as the Interregnum.</note> was called to the *Empire*: a man of meager wealth and a narrow Principality, but tracing the nobility of his lineage back to the ancient *Kings of the Franks*. *Wolfgang Lazius in* <note>Wolfgang Lazius (1514–1565) was an influential Austrian historian and physician to Ferdinand I.</note>

Because he had greatly offended the Princes of Germany, he was removed from his position. Indeed, in the Year of Christ 1297, when **Wenceslaus**, King of Bohemia, and his wife **Jutta** were being crowned again in Prague by the **Archbishop of Mainz**, a discussion took place there regarding the deposition of **Emperor Adolph**. They judged him unworthy of the empire because he had devastated churches, ravished virgins, accepted payments from the King of England <note>Adolph had accepted a large subsidy from Edward I of England to support a war against France, which he then failed to pursue, leading to accusations of corruption.</note>, and for other reasons. By common vote, they named **Albert**, Archduke of Austria, as King of the Romans. *Siffridus, Bzovius, and Calvisius for that year; Nassau Chronicle, folio 75.*

Finally, in the Year of Christ 1299 <note>Most historical records date the Battle of Göllheim and the official deposition to 1298; the author here follows a slightly different chronology.</note>, the Electors gathered again at **Mainz**, and he was cast down from the Empire for the reasons mentioned, and **Albert of Austria** was elected King. They met in battle on the **Fields of the Vangiones** <note>original: "Campis Wangionum"; a reference to the region around Worms, inhabited in antiquity by the Vangiones tribe.</note>, between **Worms** and **Speyer**. There, Adolph was slain, stripped of his life and his empire at once, after a six-hour battle that was fought for a long time with an uncertain outcome. Albert himself rode against Adolph, who was fighting with the sun in his eyes, and wounded him mortally; he was afterwards killed by the rest of the crowd. The son of Adolph was captured along with sixty Counts; many others were suffocated by the heat of the sun and the dust, and many more escaped by flight. His body was taken to the **Valley of Roses** <note>original: "Vallis Rosarum"; referring to the Cistercian monastery of Rosenthal, where Adolph was initially buried.</note>.

Therefore, having summoned the Princes to Frankfurt and delivered a solemn speech, the **Emperor** <note>original: "Cæsar"; Louis IV, also known as Louis the Bavarian</note> complained of the alleged injustices of the Popes. He set forth an account of his faith and presented and explained the **ancient laws of the Empire**. At the same time, he strove to demonstrate how the **Commonwealth of the Empire** <note>original: "Imperij Respublica"</note> does not pertain to the Bishop of Rome <note>The Pope</note> in any way. He argued that whoever is elected by the will of the Princes is in truth the Emperor, even if no papal assent or consecration intervenes; for he claimed that all of that was merely a certain ceremony. *Trithemius; Crantz, Saxonia, book 9, chapter 15; Mutius, book 24; Aventinus, book 8; Lehmann, book 7, chapter 17, and following.*

And indeed, **William of Ockham**, a Franciscan <note>A famous English philosopher and theologian who fled to Louis's court for protection</note>, as well as **Marsilius of Padua** <note>Author of "Defensor Pacis," a radical work arguing that the Emperor’s power comes from the people, not the Pope</note>, defended this Emperor against the Popes.

When he proposed conditions to the Empire that were considered ignominious, and these were rejected, he became much more bitter. He most sternly warned the Princes to elect another Emperor, even pre-defining a deadline for that matter. XXV. **Charles**, the fourth of that name and King of Bohemia, succeeded Louis. He was the son of **John** <note>John of Bohemia, known as 'the Blind'</note> and the grandson of Emperor **Henry VII**. At his baptism, he was given the name **Wenceslaus**; however, when he was confirmed by the Pope in Paris, he was called Charles by him. *Life of Charles IV.*

The beginning of his reign was turbulent. For soon after the death of Louis, the Princes held an assembly <note>a Diet</note> at **Frankfurt** and decreed that Charles IV had by no means been legitimately elected. They argued that he had purchased the votes of the **Electors** with money, and that he had not been elected in the proper place (namely, Frankfurt); furthermore, that he was not crowned at **Aachen** <note>the traditional site for imperial coronations</note>, nor was the act done openly, but in secret. They also claimed the election took place while the Empire was not yet vacant, that the legal process was not preserved, that there was no urgent cause for the election, and that it was done not for the benefit of the **Commonwealth** <note>The Holy Roman Empire</note> but out of private greed. ### XXVII. 
Robert <note>Also known as Rupert.</note> therefore, Palatine of the Rhine, brought war against Wenceslaus by means of the Marquises and Landgraves <note>Titles of nobility representing regional governors or princes.</note> of Thuringia; and Prague was besieged for a month and a half. For Wenceslaus, though already deposed, was unwilling to release the Imperial Cities from the oath of loyalty they had sworn to him; only the citizens of Nuremberg, who had gifted him with the finest wine, managed to obtain this release. <note>Wenceslaus IV was notoriously fond of wine, a trait often cited by his detractors to justify his deposition.</note> *Calvisius, Year of Christ 1401.*

Rupert also turned his mind to correcting the wrongs that Wenceslaus had committed: he refused to ratify the concessions Wenceslaus had granted to Gian Galeazzo <note>Gian Galeazzo Visconti, who had purchased the title of Duke of Milan from Wenceslaus, much to the anger of the German princes.</note> and planned to bring Lombardy <note>original: "Insubria," a classical name for the region around Milan.</note> back under the rule of the Empire. For this and other reasons, he hastened into Italy, but with almost no success. *Mutius, book 26; Aventinus, book 7.*

His reign was not so very long: for he died in the year of Christ 1410 at Oppenheim and was buried at Heidelberg.

### XXVIII. Jobst the Bearded, <note>original: "Iodocus Barbatus." Jobst of Moravia (c. 1354–1411) was a member of the House of Luxembourg and a cousin to the deposed King Wenceslaus.</note> Margrave of Moravia, succeeded Rupert in the Empire. He was the nephew of Charles IV through his brother John Henry. He was unfit for handling affairs of state, as Aeneas Sylvius <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II (1405–1464), a prominent Renaissance historian and diplomat.</note> maintains; during his entire life, he achieved nothing memorable, nor did he rule for more than five months. *Sethus Calvisius, Year of Christ 1410.* Some, however, report that he was elected King of the Romans even before Rupert, being substituted when Wenceslaus was first deposed. *Johannes Cuspinianus.* <note>Cuspinianus (1473–1529) was a humanist scholar and diplomat for the Habsburgs.</note>

His Decree survives in the works of Goldast: <note>Melchior Goldast (1578–1635), a Swiss jurist famous for compiling imperial constitutional documents.</note> That the States of the Empire may resist the Emperor himself if he acts against the Ordinances of the Empire, without being charged with any crime of rebellion or disloyalty.

### XXIX. Afterward, Sigismund, <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg (1368–1437), one of the most influential European monarchs of the late Middle Ages.</note> son of Charles IV and brother of Wenceslaus, King of Hungary and later King of Bohemia, was elected in the Year of Christ 1411. *Christoph Lehmann, last book, chapter 76:*

He took part in the Council of Constance, <note>A major ecumenical council (1414–1418) held in the German city of Konstanz (Constance).</note> which began in the Year of Christ 1414; where pilgrims numbering nearly sixty thousand people gathered. *Johannes Stumpf’s description of the great Council at Constance.* <note>original: "Iohan. Stumpffen beschreibung deß grossen Conciliumbs zu Costnitz." Stumpf was a Swiss chronicler known for his detailed historical and geographical works.</note> This council was convened against the Schisms of the three Roman Popes: <note>This refers to the Great Western Schism, a period when three rival claimants—Gregory XII, Benedict XIII, and John XXIII—all declared themselves the true Pope.</note>

In the year of Christ 1522, Rhodes yielded to them <note>original: "Rhodus ipsis cessit"; refers to the island of Rhodes falling to the Ottoman Turks under Suleiman the Magnificent</note>. He waged many wars in Italy, though through legates <note>term: legatos; here referring to his appointed commanders and representatives</note>, and even occupied Rome; and in the Castel Sant'Angelo, he held Clement <note>The text names him Clement VIII, but historically this refers to Pope Clement VII, who was besieged during the Sack of Rome in 1527</note> besieged for a long time. Even Francis, King of France, the first of that name, was captured by him and taken away to Spain. *See the histories of Lord Georg and Lord Kaspar von Frundsberg. See also Lange the Frenchman, and Guicciardini the Italian, the most prudent writers of that time. And also François Beaucaire de Péguillon, Bishop of Metz, in his commentaries on French affairs.*

But at last, in the year of Christ 1555, when he had ruled for thirty-six years, broken by cares and labors, following a new and unusual example in Roman history after Diocletian and Lothair (the son of Louis), he abdicated the Empire and the Kingdom. And indeed, he bestowed the Kingdoms upon his son Philip <note>Philip II of Spain</note>, but after two years, he transferred the Empire to his brother Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I</note>. *See David Chytraeus, and Longus, page 412.*

# UNIVERSAL HISTORY

XXXIV. **Ferdinand I**, the brother of **Charles V**, succeeded him in the Year of Christ 1558. At the beginning, however, the Pope <note>Refers to Pope Paul IV, who refused to recognize Ferdinand because Charles V had abdicated and transferred power without the Pope’s traditional involvement or permission</note> did not wish to recognize him as Emperor. *Sethus Calvisius, Year 1558. Jacques Auguste de Thou.*

Also during his reign, the name of the **Huguenots** <note>original: "Hugonotorum"; French Protestants</note> took its origin in **Tours** <note>original: "Turoni"</note>, where those devoted to the reformed religion were accustomed to meet at the gate of Hugo.

In the year 1562, the first civil war was also stirred up in France. The leader of the Catholics was **Francis of Guise**, while the leader of the Reformed Religion was **Louis of Condé**, the brother of the King of Navarre.

The **Council of Trent** was also finished in the year 1563. It had been interrupted quite often, such that eighteen years were counted from the first to the final session <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the definitive institutional response of the Catholic Church to the Protestant Reformation</note>.

In these same times occurred the **Grumbach faction** <note>term: factio Grumbachiana; a rebellion led by the knight Wilhelm von Grumbach, who sought to recover lost lands and challenged the authority of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, which threatened various movements in Germany and a dangerous lawlessness under the pretext of liberty. *Jacques Auguste de Thou.*

XXXV. **Maximilian II**, the son of Ferdinand, succeeded him in the Year of Christ 1564. He had previously been crowned King of **Bohemia**, and afterwards also King of **Hungary**. *David Chytraeus.* And finally, worn out by a complex illness, in the very Diet of **Regensburg** <note>original: "Comitijs Ratisbonensibus"; a formal deliberative assembly of the Empire</note>, in the year—

In the year **1610**, an assembly of certain States of the Empire who were of the reformed Religion was held at the beginning of the year at Hall in Swabia <note>modern-day Schwäbisch Hall</note>; they commonly call this the **Union** <note>The Protestant Union, a coalition of Protestant German states</note>. However, Matthias, having been called for help, arrived in Bohemia on the 24th of March and was crowned King of Bohemia on the 23rd of May.

XXXVIII. Ferdinand II, grandson of Ferdinand I; having been elected and crowned Emperor at Frankfurt in the year of Christ 1619 after Matthias, he holds power even now. He is a Prince who, if anyone ever was, is truly pious in the religion of his ancestors and has been successful thus far. He has indeed had a turbulent reign up to this point; however, as these movements are not yet finished, it seems they can hardly be described without those faults which Tacitus, at the beginning of Book 1 of his *Annals*, believes are inherent in the narration of recent events <note>The Roman historian Tacitus argued that history written about one's own time is often distorted by fear or favoritism; the author here suggests it is too soon to write an objective history of Ferdinand's ongoing reign</note>.

### CHAPTER XIX.

# ON THE EMPERORS
## *Of the East, after the separation of the West.*

Nicephorus Logotheta <note>original: "Nicephorus Logotheta"; Nikephoros I, who reigned 802–811 AD. However, Charlemagne soothed him with his kindness and modesty; and by exchanging gifts, both cultivated a friendship, and the definite borders of both Empires were established. *Aventinus, Book 4.* <note>Johannes Aventinus, a renowned 16th-century Bavarian historian</note>

Otherwise, Nicephorus was notorious for his wickedness and treachery, and infamous for his ever-gaping greed. Whosoever had risen from modest means to great wealth, he would accuse them of having found hidden treasure <note>Finding "buried treasure" was a common legal pretext used by rulers to confiscate private wealth</note>, and would strip them of all their fortunes. But in the Year of Christ 820, Leo lost both his life and his empire in a truly remarkable manner. On the very day of Christ’s birth <note>Christmas Day</note>, Leo was prepared to carry out the death sentence of Michael the Stammerer <note>original: *Michael Balbus*; so named for a speech impediment</note>, who had been found guilty of high treason. However, at the pleading of the Empress <note>Augusta Theodosia</note>, he postponed the punishment. On the following night, Michael the Stammerer escaped from prison and, with the assistance of a jailer, gathered a band of former conspirators. Accompanied by these men—who carried daggers hidden beneath the robes of monks—he killed the Emperor while he was singing in the choir of musicians. *Zonaras, book 3; Cedrenus; Curopalates.* <note>The Emperor Leo V was famously assassinated in the palace chapel of St. Stephen while participating in the early morning Christmas liturgy.</note>

510

V. **Michael the Stammerer** <note>original: *Balbus*; the nickname for Michael II, meaning "the stutterer"</note> was hailed as Emperor while still bound in leg-irons (for the keys to the shackles could not be found). As a follower of Constantine Copronymus <note>Constantine V, a famously strict Iconoclastic emperor</note>, he punished the Bishops who were patrons of the Holy Images with both exile and death. In other respects, that Greek Emperor was not only a "Stammerer," but also "dull-witted" <note>original: *bardus*; a Latin play on words with his nickname *Balbus*</note>. Thinking it a fine thing to understand the nature and disposition of beasts of burden, he himself possessed a very slow mind and was entirely unlearned in literature. Consequently, so that he would not see children becoming more educated than himself, he forbade them from being taught letters. After his wife died, he took a nun named Euphrosyne to be his wife. *Spondanus, Abridger of Baronius, Year of Christ 820, and Year 823, numbers 6 and 7.*

VI. After the death of Michael the Stammerer, his son **Theophilus** took up the Empire. At the very start of his reign, desiring to appear as a devotee of Justice (which historians report he always practiced in matters concerning political discipline), he ordered all those who had conspired with his father in the murder of Leo the Armenian to be punished with the penalties of parricides; he also forced his stepmother Euphrosyne to leave the court and return to the same monastery from which she came. These things are described at greater length by *Curopalates* <note>referring to the 11th-century historian John Scylitzes, who held the high court title of *Curopalates*</note>.

Likewise, when his third wife had died, he brought in a fourth named **Zoe** <note>Zoe Karbonopsina ("With the Coal-Black Eyes"). Although he did this for the sake of obtaining children—since he had raised none from his three previous wives—nevertheless, this frequent repetition of marriage was seen as a violation of <term>Canon Law</term> <note>The body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership for the government of the Christian organization.</note>. For this reason, the Patriarch of Constantinople, **Nicholas**, surnamed **the Mystic**, not only refused to bless this fourth marriage but also deposed the priest who had performed the blessing. Furthermore, he banned the Emperor himself from entering the Church. When the Patriarch, despite being asked for a long time, still refused to readmit the Emperor to the Church, he was exiled to a monastery founded by the Emperor. However, the **Roman Pontiff** <note>The Pope in Rome, who at this time was more lenient toward the Emperor's situation than the local Byzantine clergy.</note> granted a dispensation to the Emperor in this matter. *Baronius, Year of Christ 901.*

XXIX. XXX. Although she was exceptional in her virtues and therefore detested all pretense <note>original: fucum, literally "red dye" or "cosmetic," metaphorically meaning deceit or vanity</note>, she was less cherished by Manuel, who for that reason followed his wandering lusts. *Nicetas.*

He was highly commended for his administration of justice. He made no distinction between nobles or the newly promoted, the poor or the wealthy, his own associates or strangers, being accustomed to condemn anyone convicted of a fault. He wrote to the Governors and Magistrates in these very words: "Either give up your injustices, or give up your lives; for that you should act and live unjustly is neither pleasing to God, nor to be tolerated by me, His servant." <note>original: *Aut iniurias, aut vitam relinquite: Nam vos iniustè agere & viuere, né Deo gratum, nec mihi eius ministro est ferendum.*</note> Reference: Bzovius, Year of Christ 1299, number 8.

Around the year 1300, he laid the foundations of the Ottoman Empire, which he himself governed for 28 years with great wisdom and success. ### XLIII. **Andronicus III Palaeologus**, commonly called **the Junior**, the grandson of the preceding emperor, conspired against his grandfather in the Year of Christ 1320. And Bayezid <note>Bayezid I (r. 1389–1403), known as "The Thunderbolt" (*Yildirim*).</note> held Manuel <note>Manuel II Palaeologus (r. 1391–1425).</note> almost as if he were his own servant: unless Manuel gave and did everything he wanted, Bayezid would immediately become his enemy and besiege the city. Having gathered all their forces in Hungary, they marched into Thrace and arrived at Nicopolis <note>A city on the Danube in modern-day Bulgaria; the site of the last large-scale Crusade of the Middle Ages.</note>. Bayezid, hearing of their arrival, lifted his siege and set out to meet them. There, John took command of the front line for himself, against the wishes of Sigismund, the King of Hungary <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg, later Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, who had granted that position to the Prince of Wallachia <note>Mircea the Elder.</note>.

The Turks, therefore, feigned flight in the front line, and the Burgundian eagerly pursued them. But the Turks had driven stakes into the ground <note>A tactical defense called *palisades* used to break the charge of the heavy European cavalry.</note> which could not be seen by our men. When our forces reached that spot and could not proceed, and were being pressed forward by those following behind them, they were slaughtered by the Turks. Burgundy was among the first to be captured, along with many other nobles; Sigismund escaped by ship to Constantinople.

Bayezid, after such a great victory, returned to besiege Constantinople, where at last a peace was made on the condition that the Turks would have their own judge <note>term: qadi (an Islamic judge). [The Bur]gundian <note>John the Fearless (1371–1419), who led the French forces at Nicopolis.</note>, having been brought before the Turk <note>Sultan Bayezid I.</note>, was in the greatest danger of losing his life, which he nevertheless escaped. They say it happened in this way: There was a certain Physiognomist <term>Physiognomist: A practitioner of the pseudo-science of reading a person's character or future from their facial features and body.</term> among Bayezid's inner circle, from that group who profess to know the character and nature of men through their bodies, eyes, face, and brow. Having studied the captive, he advised the Emperor to release him unharmed; for he foresaw that once he returned home, he would ignite a massive fire that would burn through a large part of Europe or the Christian world. IX. In the year 1451, **Mehmed II** <note>Also known as Mehmed the Conqueror.</note> succeeded his father. He was ultimately killed by poison by his son **Selim**.

His brother **Cem** <note>original: "Zizimus"; the younger son of Mehmed II who contested the throne.</note> unsuccessfully waged war against him for the Empire; for having been defeated three times, he fled to the **Knights of Rhodes** and then to the **Roman Pope** <note>Pope Innocent VIII, who kept Cem as a hostage/political pawn.</note>. **Bayezid**, however, suffered a defeat against the Egyptians at **Tarsus** in **Cilicia**. Returning to Europe, he greatly afflicted the **Hungarians** <note>original: "Pannonios".</note> and the **Venetians** with his armies. But in **Persia**, **Ismail Safavi** <note>original: "Ismaël Sophus"; founder of the Safavid Empire.</note>, defending a heresy in religion—or rather in the Muhammadan impiety—and having gathered a most powerful force, checked the course of Turkish victory with new victories of his own. Finally, after suffering many calamities at home, **Bayezid** was attacked by his quarreling sons, who fought with fraud and violence to seize the throne; he was killed by poison at the hands of **Selim**.

XIII. **Selim II**, the son of Suleiman, succeeded him. However, in the following year, the Venetians—aided by an alliance with the Roman Pope and the King of Spain—won a memorable naval victory over the Turks <note>The Battle of Lepanto in 1571, which shattered the myth of Ottoman naval invincibility.</note>.

XIV. In the year 1574, **Murad III** <note>original: "Amurathes III".</note>, the son of Selim and another slayer of his brothers, waged most atrocious wars with the Persians as well as with the **Tatars**.

### UNIVERSAL HISTORY. 563

And so, thus far, I have briefly and without any partisan bias (the motives for which everyone who writes History should keep far away) sketched out the sequence of events from the beginning of the World in rough outline <note>original: "rudi carbone delineaui," literally "sketched with a crude piece of charcoal," a metaphor for a preliminary draft or simplified summary.</note>. This was done solely for the benefit of Students; these events may be expanded by them through constant reading and perhaps utilized in the manner of Commonplaces <term>Locorum Communium; a traditional method of study where students organized important quotes and facts under thematic headings for future use.</term>, organized according to the progression of the years.

In the first edition, I primarily followed the thread of **Johannes Sleidanus** in his *Little Book on the Four Monarchies* <note>Sleidanus was a 16th-century historian whose work on the "Four Monarchies" (Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome) was a standard textbook for understanding world history through a biblical lens.</note>. Good people will judge my work kindly; I have grown hardened against the assaults of slanderers. Having this as my one and only prayer:

->May the Lord<-
->JESUS come quickly.<-

I do not grant this praise to our departed friend <note>original: "Defuncto nostro"</note> on my own accord; his own most famous writings, which are filled in large part with historical events, demand it by their own right. Let his *Synopsis of Deeds Accomplished Since the Creation of the World* <note>original: *Synopsis rerum ab orbe condito gestarum*</note> be read. Let his *History of the East* <note>original: *Historia Orientis*</note> be leafed through, which contains the succession and deeds of the Emperors of Constantinople <note>original: "Impp. Constantinopolitanorum"; referring to the Byzantine Emperors</note> after the West was torn away, and also of the Turks, as well as the Kings of Jerusalem, and so on. Let his learned *Discourses* <note>original: *Discursus*</note> be consulted regarding the diverse nature of peoples, and the characters of men and nations, which are usually formed primarily by the geographic location of their region. Those who knew the departed in familiar conversation will testify that nothing concerning the deeds of the ancients, and nothing of antiquity, could be brought forward that would seem new to Besoldus.
